corp-posh.title: POSH at work: safe, respectful workplaces
corp-posh.description: A complete, chapter-by-chapter guide to India's Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 — what harassment is, the Internal Committee, the complaint process, and how employees, bystanders and managers act well.

courses.title: Ch 1 · What sexual harassment at work means
courses.summary: The history behind the POSH Act, its exact definition of sexual harassment, the circumstances that make conduct harassment, and who and where the law covers.
outcomes: Learners can explain why the Act exists and how it grew out of the Vishaka guidelines
Learners can list the kinds of conduct the Act calls sexual harassment
Learners can tell quid-pro-quo harassment from a hostile work environment
Learners can decide whether a place, person and situation fall within the Act

scenes.text: On her first day, Ananya sits through a POSH session and wonders: why does a company need a special law for this?
The trainer explains that until 1997 India had no workplace-specific rule — women had to rely on general criminal law.
A Supreme Court case changed that, and in 2013 Parliament turned those guidelines into a full law.

steps.title: From Vishaka to the Act
steps.body:
In **Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)** the Supreme Court said that sexual harassment at work violates women's fundamental rights to equality, to practise any profession, and to life with dignity (Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21). Because there was no law, the Court laid down binding **Vishaka guidelines** for employers.

In **2013** Parliament passed the **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013**, usually called the **POSH Act**. Rules under it were notified the same year.

steps.title: Three words in the title
steps.body:
- **Prevention** — awareness, policy, training, so harassment does not happen.
- **Prohibition** — the conduct is forbidden; employers must not allow it.
- **Redressal** — a fast, fair, confidential way to complain and get remedies.

steps.title: Who carries the duty
steps.body: The Act puts the main duty on the **employer**: frame a policy, set up an **Internal Committee** (commonly called the ICC or IC), train people, display information, and act on the committee's recommendations. Government also has duties — each district has a **District Officer** and a **Local Committee**.

steps.title: Solved example: civil route vs criminal route
steps.body:
**Situation:** a colleague repeatedly sends sexual jokes to a woman co-worker.

**Step 1:** Is it at a workplace and sexual in nature? Yes — civil remedy under the POSH Act through the Internal Committee.
**Step 2:** Is it also a crime? Sexual harassment is also an offence under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Section 75)**, which replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.
**Step 3:** The two routes are separate: she may use one or both. The committee can also help her file a police complaint if she wishes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking POSH is only an HR formality — it is a law with penalties for employers.
- Thinking it applies only to big companies — every workplace is covered; small ones use the Local Committee.
- Citing old IPC sections as current law — the criminal side is now the BNS.

steps.title: Good to know
steps.body: Many companies make their own policy **gender-neutral** (protecting everyone), which is good practice. The Act itself protects **women**. This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Put these milestones in order.

events.text: Supreme Court lays down the Vishaka guidelines
POSH Act passed and Rules notified
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita comes into force (1 July), replacing the IPC

quiz.q: Which case first gave binding guidelines on workplace sexual harassment in India?
quiz.why: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) laid down the binding guidelines on workplace sexual harassment, which the 2013 Act later replaced.

quiz.q: The POSH Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The POSH Act was passed in 2013, as its full name shows: the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Who has the primary duty to set up an Internal Committee?
quiz.why: The employer has the duty to constitute the Internal Committee. The victim, police and union don't.

quiz.q: Workplace sexual harassment is also a criminal offence under which current law?
quiz.why: Workplace sexual harassment is also a criminal offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.

options: Getting a remedy for a complaint
quiz.why: 'Redressal' means getting a remedy for a complaint, through a fair process.

scenes.text: In the team WhatsApp group, Rohit keeps posting 'funny' memes with sexual content and tagging Priya.
Priya has said she doesn't find them funny. He says, 'Relax, everyone does it.'
Is this harassment if he never touched anyone? The Act answers clearly.

steps.title: The Act's list
The key word: unwelcome
steps.body: The test is whether the conduct is **unwelcome to the woman**, not whether the other person 'meant it as a joke'. **Impact matters more than intent.** Silence or not protesting in the moment does not mean the conduct was welcome — power differences often make people stay quiet.

steps.title: Verbal and non-verbal
steps.body: Non-verbal conduct includes leering, sexual gestures, sending sexual images, stickers or memes, and stalking-like attention. Verbal includes comments on body or clothes with sexual overtones, sexual jokes, questions about someone's sex life, and repeated requests for dates after a clear 'no'.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
**Case:** A manager tells a junior, 'You'd get more clients if you dressed sexier.'
**Step 1:** Sexual in nature? Yes — sexually coloured remark.
**Step 2:** Unwelcome? She objects and feels humiliated.
**Step 3:** Conclusion: falls within the definition; she can complain to the Internal Committee.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
**Case:** A colleague says, 'Great presentation, well done.'
**Step 1:** Sexual in nature? No.
**Step 2:** Conclusion: not sexual harassment. Ordinary professional praise is fine. (Rudeness or bullying that is not sexual may still breach the company's Code of Conduct, but it is not POSH.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'There was no touching, so it's not harassment' — wrong; remarks, images and gestures count.
- 'It happened only once' — a single serious act can be harassment.
- 'She laughed along' — laughing to avoid conflict is not consent.

activity.prompt: Sort each behaviour.

items.text: Repeated sexual jokes in team chat after being asked to stop
Sending an explicit video to a colleague
Asking for a date again and again after a clear no
Hinting a promotion depends on 'spending time together'
Giving honest feedback on a report
Inviting the whole team to lunch
Assigning a deadline the person dislikes

quiz.q: The central test for sexual harassment under the Act is whether the conduct is:
quiz.why: The central test is whether the conduct is unwelcome and sexual in nature. Repetition, intent to joke and seniority aren't required.

quiz.q: Which is listed in the Act?
quiz.why: Showing pornography is one of the acts listed in the definition. Salary cuts, dress codes and deadlines are not sexual conduct.

quiz.q: Sending sexual memes to a colleague is:
options: Never harassment because it is online
Non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature that can be harassment
quiz.why: Sending sexual memes is non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature, which can be harassment even online.

quiz.q: A woman stays silent during an inappropriate comment. This means:
quiz.why: Silence is not consent and doesn't make the conduct welcome. The complaint remains valid.

quiz.q: Can a single incident be sexual harassment?
quiz.why: Yes. A single incident can meet the definition; repetition is not required.

lessons.title: Quid pro quo and hostile environment

scenes.text: Before appraisal, Meena's team lead says, 'Your rating depends on how friendly you are with me after hours.'
Elsewhere, Kavya's floor has posters and banter of a sexual kind every day; she dreads coming to office.
Both situations are covered — in two different ways.

steps.title: Circumstances in the Act
Quid pro quo ('this for that')
steps.body: A benefit (rating, promotion, project, leave) is offered or a harm (bad rating, transfer, firing) is threatened in exchange for sexual compliance. It is usually done by someone with **power** over the woman — but power can be informal too (a senior client, a key colleague).

steps.title: Hostile work environment
steps.body: Sexual conduct that makes the workplace intimidating or offensive, even with no 'deal' attached — e.g. constant sexual comments, explicit screensavers, a group that rates women's looks. It can come from peers, juniors, vendors or clients.

steps.title: Solved example: classify
steps.body:
**Case A:** 'Come to dinner with me alone or forget the onsite trip.' → threat of detrimental treatment + promise of benefit → **quid pro quo**.
**Case B:** Colleagues comment daily on a woman's body; nobody threatens her job → **hostile environment**.
**Case C:** A client repeatedly messages a woman consultant with sexual remarks → covered; the employer must help her act even though the client is an outsider.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing harassment needs a boss — peers and clients can harass too.
- Thinking a hint is safe because nothing was 'said directly' — the Act covers **implied** promises and threats.
- Ignoring the environment test because 'no one complained before'.

activity.prompt: Match each case to the circumstance it shows.
pairs: 'Be nice to me and you'll get the best rating'
'Refuse and you'll be moved to night shift'
Explicit posters and sexual banter every day
Public sexual mockery that affects her health

options: A benefit or harm tied to sexual compliance
quiz.why: Quid pro quo means 'this for that': a benefit or harm is tied to sexual compliance.

quiz.q: Can a client harass an employee under the Act's protection?
options: Yes, the employer must still help her act
Only if the client is in India
quiz.why: The aggrieved woman is protected regardless of who the respondent is; the employer must assist.

quiz.q: A hint (not a direct statement) about promotion in return for sexual favours is:
quiz.why: A hint about promotion in return for sexual favours is covered as an implied promise. The Act covers promises and threats by implication.
Daily sexual comments by peers create a hostile environment, a pervasive offensive atmosphere. A tough deadline or strict manager is not harassment.

options: Seniors, peers, juniors, clients or vendors
quiz.why: Harassment can come from seniors, peers, juniors, clients or vendors, because anyone can be a respondent.

lessons.title: Who is protected and what is a 'workplace'

scenes.text: After a late release, a company cab drops Sneha home. The driver makes sexual remarks all the way.
Her friend Divya works from home; a colleague keeps turning video calls into sexual 'jokes'.
Neither was in the office building. Are they covered?

steps.title: Aggrieved woman
steps.body: The Act protects an **aggrieved woman** — a woman **of any age, whether employed or not**, who alleges harassment at a workplace. So interns, trainees, contract and temporary staff, consultants, visitors, customers and job applicants are all protected. A **domestic worker** is also protected (her complaint goes to the Local Committee).

steps.title: Workplace — wider than the office
steps.body: 'Workplace' includes the organisation's premises and **any place visited by the employee arising out of or during employment, including transportation provided by the employer** for that journey. Practically this covers client sites, offsite events, conferences, hotels on work trips, company cabs, and — as most policies now state — virtual meetings and chats used for work.

steps.title: Employee — also wide
steps.body: An 'employee' under the Act includes regular, temporary, ad hoc or daily-wage workers, whether employed directly or through an agent or contractor, with or without pay, and includes trainees, apprentices and probationers.

steps.title: Solved example: is it covered?
steps.body:
**Sneha in the company cab:** transport provided by the employer for work → workplace → covered.
**Divya on work video calls:** conduct arising out of employment, on the work platform → treated as within the workplace by most policies and committees → covered.
**A woman harassed by a stranger at a mall on a Sunday:** not linked to work → not POSH (but criminal law applies; call 112 in an emergency).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Interns can't complain' — they can.
- 'The office party was after hours, so it's private' — company-organised events are work-linked.
- 'Only employees of our company are protected' — a visiting vendor's employee or a customer is also protected while at your workplace.

This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: A 19-year-old unpaid intern is protected by the Act.
statements.why: Employees include trainees and unpaid workers; any woman at the workplace is protected.

statements.s: A company cab is never part of the workplace.
A job applicant harassed during an interview is protected.
statements.why: An aggrieved woman need not be employed.

statements.s: Domestic workers are excluded from the Act.
statements.why: They are covered; complaints go to the Local Committee.

statements.s: A client-site visit is part of the workplace.
statements.why: Places visited during employment are included.

quiz.q: 'Aggrieved woman' under the Act means a woman:
options: Of any age, employed or not, at a workplace
quiz.why: An 'aggrieved woman' is a woman of any age, employed or not, at a workplace. The definition is deliberately wide.

quiz.q: Which is a workplace under the Act?
options: A cinema on a holiday with friends
quiz.why: An employer-provided cab for work travel is part of the workplace. A random mall, a neighbour's house or a cinema on holiday is not.

quiz.q: A contract worker supplied by an agency is:
quiz.why: A contract worker supplied by an agency is an employee for POSH purposes, since workers engaged through contractors are included.

quiz.q: Where does a domestic worker complain?
quiz.why: A domestic worker's complaint goes to the Local Committee, not a company's Internal Committee.

quiz.q: Harassment during an offsite team event is:
options: Only if alcohol was not served
quiz.why: Harassment at an offsite team event is within the workplace concept, because work-linked events are included.

questions.q: POSH stands for prevention of sexual harassment; the Act's full name includes 'Prevention, Prohibition and ___'.
questions.why: The full name is the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act.

questions.q: The Vishaka guidelines were laid down in:
questions.why: The Vishaka guidelines were laid down in 1997, in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan.

questions.q: Which is NOT in the Act's list of sexual harassment?
options: Giving a low rating for poor work with evidence
questions.why: Giving a low rating for poor work with evidence is fair performance feedback, not sexual conduct. Remarks, favours and pornography are listed acts.

questions.q: The main test for whether conduct is harassment is:
options: Whether it is unwelcome and sexual
questions.why: The main test is whether the conduct is unwelcome and sexual. Impact matters more than the respondent's intention.

questions.q: A trainee, a visitor and a job applicant — who can be an 'aggrieved woman'?
questions.why: All three can be an 'aggrieved woman', since the Act covers any woman at a workplace, employed or not.

questions.q: Which of these is part of 'workplace'?
options: Company cab to a client site
A friend's wedding unrelated to work
questions.why: A company cab to a client site is part of the workplace, as employer transport during work journeys. A friend's wedding or personal gym isn't.

questions.q: 'If you want the onsite opportunity, be friendly with me after work' is an example of:
options: Promise of preferential treatment (quid pro quo)
questions.why: 'Be friendly with me after work' for an onsite opportunity ties a benefit to sexual compliance, which is quid pro quo, a promise of preferential treatment.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A peer can sexually harass a colleague. Reason (R): The Act requires the respondent to be her supervisor.
options: A and R true, R explains A
questions.why: A is true and R is false: a peer can harass a colleague, and the Act doesn't require the respondent to be a supervisor.

questions.q: Case: Riya laughs awkwardly at a colleague's sexual comment in a meeting, then later complains. The colleague says she laughed, so it was welcome. The best view is:
options: Awkward laughter does not make conduct welcome; the committee looks at the whole context
questions.why: Awkward laughter doesn't make conduct welcome, since reactions under social pressure aren't consent. The committee looks at the whole context.

questions.q: Criminal sexual harassment is now an offence under:
questions.why: Under the current criminal law, sexual harassment is an offence under BNS Section 75, which replaced IPC 354A from 1 July 2024.

questions.q: Explicit screensavers and daily sexual banter on a floor, with no threats, most closely fit:
questions.why: Explicit screensavers and daily sexual banter, even without threats, create an offensive sexual atmosphere, so they fit a hostile work environment.

questions.q: Case: A woman consultant is harassed over chat by a client's manager. Her employer says 'he's not our staff, we can't help.' Which is correct?
options: The employer should assist her, including taking up the matter with the client and helping her complain
questions.why: Employers must assist the aggrieved woman even when the respondent is a third party.

questions.q: Which statement is most accurate about the Act and gender?
options: The Act protects women; many company policies extend protection to all genders
Policies cannot go beyond the Act
The Act protects everyone equally by its text
questions.why: The Act protects women, but many company policies extend protection to all genders, which is good practice. Policies can go beyond the Act.

questions.q: Case: Harassment happened over a work video call while both worked from home. The respondent argues 'home is not a workplace'. The stronger argument is:
options: Conduct arising out of employment on work platforms is treated as within the workplace
questions.why: Conduct arising out of employment on work platforms, like a work video call, is treated as within the workplace. The workplace concept follows the work, not only the building.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Harassment by implication is covered. Reason (R): The Act covers implied as well as explicit promises and threats.
options: A and R true, R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: the Act covers promises and threats made directly or by implication, so harassment by implication is covered.

questions.q: Which combination best captures why the Supreme Court acted in 1997?
options: Article 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 rights were being violated with no specific law
questions.why: The Supreme Court acted in 1997 because fundamental rights under Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 were being violated and there was no specific law.

courses.title: Ch 2 · The Internal Committee and Local Committee
courses.summary: How the Internal Committee is formed, what the Local Committee does, the powers committees have, and the employer's duties and penalties.
outcomes: Learners can state the composition rules of an Internal Committee
Learners can explain when the Local Committee is used
Learners can describe committee powers and independence
Learners can list employer duties and penalties for non-compliance

scenes.text: Arjun's startup has just hired its 10th employee. His HR adviser says, 'You now need an Internal Committee.'
Arjun plans to make himself, his co-founder and his friend the members.
The adviser shakes her head: 'That won't be valid. Let me show you the rules.'

steps.title: When it is required
steps.body: Every employer with **10 or more employees** must constitute an **Internal Committee** by written order. If there are offices or units at different places, a committee should be set up at **each** administrative unit or office.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body:
- **Presiding Officer:** a woman employed at a **senior level** (if none, from another office or unit of the same employer).
- **At least two members** from among employees, preferably committed to the cause of women or with social-work experience or legal knowledge.
- **One external member** from an NGO or association committed to women's cause, or a person familiar with sexual harassment issues.
- **At least one-half** of the total members must be **women**.
- Members hold office for up to **3 years**.

steps.title: Solved example: check validity
steps.body:
**Proposed IC:** Presiding Officer — Ms Rao (VP, woman); members — Mr Shah (engineer), Ms Iyer (HR); external — Ms Thomas (NGO).
**Step 1:** Senior woman presiding? ✔
**Step 2:** ≥ 2 employee members? ✔ (Shah, Iyer)
**Step 3:** External member? ✔
**Step 4:** Women ≥ half? Rao, Iyer, Thomas = 3 of 4 ✔
**Result:** valid.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the flaw
steps.body:
**Proposed IC:** Founder (man) presiding, co-founder (man), friend (man, outsider).
**Flaws:** presiding officer must be a senior woman; no external member from a women's cause background; women are 0% (< half). **Invalid.** Recommendations from an invalidly formed committee can be challenged.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making the founder or MD a member — the person with ultimate power over outcomes should not sit in judgement; it also undermines trust.
- Forgetting the external member.
- Not renewing members after their term ends.
- One committee for a company with offices in five cities without considering each unit.

activity.prompt: IC validity checklist
items: Employer has 10 or more employees → IC required
Presiding Officer is a senior-level woman
One external member from a women's-cause NGO or with relevant expertise
At least half the members are women
Constituted by written order; term not over 3 years
Names and contacts displayed at the workplace

quiz.q: An Internal Committee is required when an employer has at least:
quiz.why: An Internal Committee is required when an employer has 10 or more employees.
The Presiding Officer must be a senior-level woman employee.

quiz.q: What proportion of members must be women?
quiz.why: At least one-half of the members must be women.

quiz.q: The external member should be from:
options: An NGO/association committed to women's cause or familiar with sexual harassment issues
quiz.why: The external member comes from an NGO or association committed to women's cause or familiar with sexual harassment issues. This brings independence and expertise.
IC members serve a term of up to 3 years.

lessons.title: The Local Committee and District Officer

scenes.text: Lata works in a boutique with six staff. The owner himself makes sexual remarks.
There's no committee, and the harasser is the boss. Where can she go?
The answer: her district's Local Committee.

steps.title: District Officer
steps.body: The appropriate government notifies a **District Officer** (often a District Magistrate, Collector or similar officer) for each district. The District Officer constitutes the **Local Committee (LC)** and appoints **nodal officers** at block, taluka and ward levels to receive complaints and forward them to the LC within **7 days**.

steps.title: When the Local Committee is used
steps.body:
- The establishment has **fewer than 10 employees** (so no IC).
- The complaint is **against the employer** himself or herself.
- The woman is a **domestic worker** or works in the unorganised sector.

steps.title: LC composition (summary)
steps.body: The LC has a **chairperson** — an eminent woman in the field of social work committed to women's cause; a member who is a woman working in the block/taluka/municipality of the district; two members from NGOs committed to women's cause (at least one a woman, with preference for legal knowledge), with at least one member from a Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe, OBC or minority community; and an officer dealing with social welfare or women and child development as an ex-officio member.

steps.title: Solved example: route the complaint
steps.body:
**Case 1:** Factory with 300 workers; complaint against a supervisor → **IC** of the factory.
**Case 2:** Same factory; complaint against the owner-employer → **LC**.
**Case 3:** Domestic worker harassed by the householder → **LC**.
**Case 4:** Café with 7 employees → **LC**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Small firms are exempt' — no; their workers use the LC.
- 'You can't complain about the owner' — you can, to the LC.

This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Which committee hears the complaint?

items.text: IT firm, 2,000 staff, complaint against a team lead
Shop with 4 employees
Domestic worker against her employer
Company of 40 staff, complaint against the company's proprietor
Bank branch, complaint against a co-worker

quiz.why: The District Officer constitutes the Local Committee.

quiz.q: A complaint against the employer himself goes to:
quiz.why: A complaint against the employer himself goes to the Local Committee, to avoid a conflict of interest.

quiz.q: Nodal officers must forward complaints to the LC within:
quiz.why: Nodal officers must forward complaints to the Local Committee within 7 days.

options: An eminent woman in social work committed to women's cause
quiz.why: The LC is chaired by an eminent woman in social work committed to women's cause, as the Act's composition rules require.
A café with 7 staff has fewer than 10 employees, so it uses the Local Committee.

scenes.text: The IC asks a key witness, a vendor's employee, to attend. He ignores the email.
The respondent refuses to share chat logs he says are 'private'.
The Presiding Officer reminds everyone: the committee has the powers of a civil court for these matters.

steps.title: Civil-court powers
Independence
steps.body: Members must act **impartially**. A member with a conflict (e.g. a close friend of a party, or reporting to the respondent) should **recuse**. The committee's quorum under the Rules is at least three members including the Presiding Officer. Management should not pressure the committee; good companies give it budget, training and access to legal support.

steps.title: Solved example: a conflict of interest
steps.body:
**Case:** An IC member is the respondent's direct manager.
**Step 1:** Can she be impartial? There is a reasonable doubt.
**Step 2:** Action: she declares the conflict and steps aside; the inquiry continues with a valid quorum (≥3 incl. Presiding Officer).
**Step 3:** Record the recusal in the minutes.

steps.title: Natural justice in one line
steps.body: Hear **both sides**, give each a chance to present evidence and respond, decide on evidence, give reasons, and keep it confidential.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the IC as an HR investigation team that reports to management — it is a statutory body.
- Members discussing the case in the cafeteria — a confidentiality breach.
- Skipping the respondent's side to 'protect' the complainant — unfair and makes the outcome vulnerable.

statements.s: The IC can summon a witness and examine them on oath.
statements.why: It has civil-court powers for this.

statements.s: An IC member who is the respondent's best friend should still sit on the case.
statements.why: A conflict of interest requires recusal.

statements.s: The committee can require documents such as chat logs to be produced.
The CEO can overrule the IC's process by email.
statements.why: The IC is a statutory body; it must act independently.

quiz.q: The IC's powers during inquiry are similar to those of a:
quiz.why: During inquiry, the IC has powers similar to a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, such as summoning witnesses.

quiz.q: Minimum quorum for an inquiry under the Rules:
options: Three members including the Presiding Officer
quiz.why: The Rules require a quorum of at least three members, including the Presiding Officer.

quiz.q: A member with a conflict should:
quiz.why: A member with a conflict should declare it and recuse, to preserve fairness.
Natural justice requires hearing both sides before deciding.

options: Sharing the report with the parties as required
Discussing case details with colleagues at lunch
quiz.why: Discussing case details with colleagues at lunch is a confidentiality breach. Case details must not be disclosed.

scenes.text: An auditor visits a mid-size company. There is a POSH policy PDF on the intranet, but no posters, no training records and no annual report.
'You may be exposed to penalties,' she warns.
The HR head makes a plan that afternoon.

steps.title: Employer duties (Section 19)
Annual report
steps.body: The IC (or LC) prepares an **annual report** each calendar year and submits it to the employer and the **District Officer**. Under the Rules it includes the number of complaints received, disposed of, pending beyond 90 days, workshops held, and action taken. Companies covered by company law also disclose POSH compliance in their Board's report.

steps.title: Penalty (Section 26)
steps.body: If an employer fails to constitute an IC, fails to act on recommendations, or contravenes other provisions, the employer is punishable with a **fine up to ₹50,000**. On a **repeat** offence: up to **twice** the punishment, and possible **cancellation or non-renewal of licence or registration** needed to run the business.

steps.title: Solved example: fix the audit gaps
steps.body:
**Gaps:** no posters, no training, no annual report.
**Step 1:** Display IC names, contacts and penal consequences in every office and on the intranet.
**Step 2:** Schedule mandatory awareness training for all, plus separate IC-member and manager training.
**Step 3:** IC drafts the annual report for the calendar year and files it with the District Officer.
**Step 4:** Keep records (attendance, minutes) as evidence of compliance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A policy on paper with no training or posters — duties are not met.
- Ignoring IC recommendations because the respondent is a 'star performer' — this itself attracts penalty.

This is general education, not legal advice.

Constitute the IC by written order (with external member)

quiz.q: Maximum fine for a first contravention by an employer:
quiz.why: The maximum fine for a first contravention by an employer is ₹50,000.

quiz.q: For a repeat offence the employer may face:
options: Up to twice the punishment and possible licence cancellation
quiz.why: For a repeat offence the employer may face up to twice the punishment and possible cancellation of licence or registration (Section 26).

quiz.q: The IC's annual report goes to the employer and the:
quiz.why: The IC's annual report goes to the employer and the District Officer.

options: Make complainants sign NDAs about the law
Display penal consequences and IC details
quiz.why: Displaying penal consequences and IC details is an employer duty under Section 19. Employers can't charge complaint fees or decide cases personally.

quiz.q: If a woman wants to go to the police, the employer should:
quiz.why: If a woman wants to go to the police, the employer should assist her, as the Act requires.

questions.q: Minimum number of employees at which an IC becomes mandatory:
questions.why: An IC becomes mandatory at 10 or more employees.

questions.q: Who presides over an IC?
questions.why: An IC is presided over by a senior-level woman employee.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Complaint, conciliation and inquiry
courses.summary: How a complaint is made, time limits, conciliation, interim relief, how a fair inquiry runs, timelines, outcomes, compensation, false complaints, appeal and confidentiality.
outcomes: Learners can explain how and when a complaint is filed
Learners can describe conciliation and interim relief
Learners can outline the inquiry steps and statutory timelines
Learners can explain possible outcomes, appeal and confidentiality rules

scenes.text: For two months a senior has sent Nisha sexual messages. She has saved screenshots.
She is unsure how to write a complaint or whether it's 'too late'.
The Presiding Officer offers to help her put it in writing — the Act requires that help.

steps.title: Time limit
steps.body: The aggrieved woman may make a complaint **in writing** to the IC (or LC) **within 3 months** from the date of the incident — and for a **series** of incidents, within 3 months from the **last** incident. The committee may **extend** this by up to **another 3 months** if satisfied that circumstances prevented her from filing earlier, recording reasons in writing.

steps.title: Help to write
steps.body: If she cannot write the complaint, the Presiding Officer or any member must render **reasonable assistance** to her to make it in writing. Under the Rules she typically submits **six copies** with supporting documents and names and addresses of witnesses.

steps.title: When someone else can file
steps.body: If she is unable to complain because of physical or mental incapacity, death or otherwise, the Rules allow certain persons to file: e.g. a relative or friend, a co-worker, an officer of the National or State Commission for Women, or a person with knowledge of the incident — with her written consent where required; and in case of death, her legal heir.

steps.title: Solved example: is it in time?
steps.body:
**Incidents:** 5 Jan, 20 Feb and 10 March.
**Step 1:** It is a series → count from the last incident, 10 March.
**Step 2:** 3 months → around 10 June.
**Step 3:** She files on 25 July. The IC may extend up to 3 more months (to around 10 September) if she shows sufficient cause (e.g. fear, illness), recording reasons.
**Result:** can be admitted with a reasoned extension.

steps.title: What a good complaint contains
steps.body:
- Who, what, when, where — specific dates, places and words used.
- Evidence: screenshots, emails, call logs, diary notes made at the time.
- Names of witnesses or people she told.
- What she wants (e.g. stop, transfer, action).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Waiting for 'enough' evidence while the time limit runs out — file and give what you have.
- Deleting chats out of disgust — export or screenshot first.
- Thinking an anonymous email is a formal complaint — the Act expects a written complaint by or on behalf of the aggrieved woman; companies may still look into anonymous concerns under other policies.

activity.prompt: Last incident in a series was on 1 April. Ignoring extensions, roughly how many months does she have to file?

quiz.q: Normal time limit to file a complaint:
quiz.why: A complaint should normally be filed within 3 months.

quiz.q: For a series of incidents, the period counts from:
quiz.why: For a series of incidents, the 3 months count from the last incident.

quiz.q: The committee can extend the time limit by up to:
quiz.why: The committee can extend the time limit by up to another 3 months, recording its reasons.

quiz.q: If the woman cannot write the complaint herself:
options: IC members must help her put it in writing
quiz.why: If the woman cannot write the complaint herself, IC members must help her put it in writing.

quiz.q: Best first step with harassing chat messages:
quiz.why: Preserve harassing chat messages as evidence. Deleting them or replying angrily weakens the case.

story.title: She just wants it to stop

scenes.text: Farah tells the IC: 'I don't want him fired. I just want a written apology and for it to stop.'
Meanwhile she still reports to him every day, which feels unsafe.
The Act has tools for both needs.

steps.title: Conciliation (Section 10)
steps.body:
Before starting an inquiry, the IC may — **only at the request of the aggrieved woman** — take steps to settle the matter through **conciliation**. Key rules:
- **No monetary settlement** can be the basis of conciliation.
- If a settlement is reached, the IC records it and sends it to the employer for action; copies go to both parties.
- Once settled, no further inquiry is held — but if the respondent **does not comply** with the terms, she can inform the IC and the inquiry proceeds.

steps.title: Interim relief (Section 12)
Solved example: Farah
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Farah requests conciliation in writing → IC facilitates; the respondent agrees to apologise in writing, stop all contact outside work tasks, and complete training. No money involved ✔.
**Step 2:** For safety until things settle, she requests that he not write her appraisal → IC recommends another manager does it.
**Step 3:** Two months later he messages her again → she informs the IC → inquiry begins.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- HR 'suggesting' conciliation to close the file fast — it must be her choice.
- Offering money to settle — not allowed as the basis.
- Transferring the complainant against her wishes as 'relief' — interim relief is to protect her, on her request.

statements.s: The IC can start conciliation on its own without the woman's request.
A ₹2 lakh payment can be the basis of conciliation.
statements.why: No monetary settlement as the basis.

statements.s: Interim leave can be up to 3 months, in addition to normal leave.
If the respondent breaks the settlement terms, the inquiry can proceed.
statements.why: She can inform the IC, which then inquires.

quiz.why: Conciliation can be initiated only at the aggrieved woman's request.

quiz.q: Which cannot be the basis of conciliation?
quiz.why: A monetary settlement can't be the basis of conciliation. Apology, no-contact commitments and training can.

options: During the inquiry on her written request
quiz.why: Interim relief can be given during the inquiry, on her written request (Section 12).

quiz.q: Maximum special leave as interim relief:
quiz.why: Special leave as interim relief can be up to 3 months.

quiz.q: Restraining the respondent from writing her appraisal is:
quiz.why: Restraining the respondent from writing her appraisal is a form of interim relief. It isn't a punishment before the inquiry.

lessons.title: Running a fair inquiry: steps and timelines

scenes.text: The IC receives a complaint on 1 June. The Presiding Officer opens a case file.
She maps the deadlines: notice, reply, hearings, report.
Both sides will be heard, and the inquiry must finish within 90 days.

steps.title: Key timelines
steps.body:
- IC sends a copy of the complaint to the respondent within **7 working days** of receiving it (Rules).
- Respondent files a reply with documents and witness list within **10 working days** of receiving the copy (Rules).
- Inquiry to be **completed within 90 days**.
- IC gives its **report to the employer within 10 days** of completing the inquiry, and copies to both parties.
- Employer **acts on the recommendations within 60 days** of receiving the report.

steps.title: How hearings run
steps.body: The IC hears each side, examines witnesses, reviews documents, and may allow each party to respond to the other's evidence. Under the Rules, **legal practitioners are not allowed** to represent parties at any stage of the IC/LC proceedings. The IC may proceed **ex parte** (or terminate) if a party is absent for **three consecutive hearings** without sufficient cause, after giving 15 days' written notice.

steps.title: Solved example: timeline math
steps.body:
Complaint received **1 June**.
**Step 1:** Copy to respondent within 7 working days → by about 10 June.
**Step 2:** Reply within 10 working days of receipt.
**Step 3:** Inquiry must finish within 90 days of the complaint → about **30 August**.
**Step 4:** Report within 10 days → about **9 September**.
**Step 5:** Employer acts within 60 days of the report → about **8 November**.

steps.title: Standard of proof
steps.body: An IC inquiry is a domestic/civil inquiry: findings are made on the **preponderance of probabilities** (what is more likely than not, on the evidence), not 'beyond reasonable doubt' as in criminal trials.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not giving the respondent the complaint copy or chance to reply — breaches natural justice.
- Letting hearings drift past 90 days.
- Asking the complainant intrusive questions about her past or clothing — irrelevant and re-traumatising.

activity.prompt: Put the inquiry stages in order.
items: Written complaint received by the IC
Copy sent to respondent (within 7 working days)

quiz.q: The inquiry must be completed within:
quiz.why: The inquiry must be completed within 90 days.

quiz.q: After the inquiry, the report goes to the employer within:
quiz.why: After the inquiry, the report goes to the employer within 10 days.

quiz.q: The employer must act on recommendations within:
quiz.why: The employer must act on the recommendations within 60 days.

quiz.q: Can lawyers represent parties before the IC?
options: No, the Rules do not allow legal practitioners
quiz.why: The Rules don't allow legal practitioners to represent parties before the IC or LC.
IC findings use the preponderance of probabilities, a civil standard, not beyond reasonable doubt.

scenes.text: The IC finds the allegation proved against Vikram and recommends action.
It also recommends compensation to the complainant, deducted from his salary.
Vikram says he will appeal. Both parties must keep everything confidential.

steps.title: If the allegation is not proved
steps.body: The IC recommends to the employer that **no action** is required in the matter.

steps.title: If the allegation is proved (Section 13)
Deciding compensation (Section 15)
steps.body: The committee considers: the **mental trauma, pain, suffering and emotional distress** caused; **loss in career opportunity**; **medical expenses** for physical or psychiatric treatment; the **income and financial status** of the respondent; and whether payment in a **lump sum or instalments** is feasible.

steps.title: False or malicious complaints (Section 14)
steps.body: If the IC concludes a complaint was **malicious** or made knowing it was false, or that forged/misleading documents were produced, it may recommend action against the complainant. **But mere inability to substantiate a complaint or provide adequate proof is not grounds for action.** A malicious intent must be established after an inquiry. Similar action is possible against a witness who gives false evidence.

steps.title: Confidentiality and appeal
steps.body:
**Section 16:** the contents of the complaint, identities and addresses of the woman, respondent and witnesses, inquiry proceedings, recommendations and action taken must **not be published or made known** to the public, press or media. Information about the justice secured may be shared without revealing identities. Breach can be penalised under service rules (the Rules prescribe recovering a sum of ₹5,000).
**Section 18:** a person aggrieved by the recommendations may **appeal** to the court or tribunal under service rules (or as prescribed) **within 90 days** of the recommendations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Punishing a complainant just because evidence was weak — prohibited.
- Posting about the case on social media 'to warn others' with names — breaches confidentiality.
- Treating compensation as optional extra when the case is proved — it is a standard consideration.

This is general education, not legal advice.

a.text: You are an IC member. The complaint could not be proved — evidence was thin, but nothing suggests she lied. A manager says, 'Recommend action against her for wasting our time.' What do you do?

choices.label: Recommend action for a false complaint
choices.feedback: Inability to prove is not malice.

choices.label: Recommend no action against either party, and suggest awareness training for the team

b.text: The Act says mere inability to substantiate is not a ground for action. Doing this would deter genuine complaints. Reconsider?

c.text: You record 'allegation not proved; no action required' and suggest preventive training. Confidentiality is maintained. Fair and lawful.

quiz.q: If the allegation is not proved, the IC recommends:
quiz.why: If the allegation is not proved, the IC recommends that no action is required.

quiz.q: Which is a Section 15 factor for compensation?
quiz.why: Loss in career opportunity is a Section 15 factor for deciding compensation, along with trauma and medical expenses.

quiz.q: Inability to provide adequate proof means:
options: Not by itself grounds for action against the complainant
quiz.why: Inability to provide adequate proof isn't by itself grounds for action against the complainant (Section 14 proviso).

quiz.q: Appeal against recommendations must be filed within:
quiz.why: An appeal against the recommendations must be filed within 90 days.

quiz.q: Sharing complainant identity with the media is:
quiz.why: Sharing a complainant's identity with the media is prohibited under Section 16, the confidentiality rule.

questions.q: A complaint must normally be filed within:
questions.why: A complaint must normally be filed within 3 months.

questions.q: A complaint must be made:
questions.why: A complaint must be made in writing, and the committee helps if she can't write.

questions.q: Conciliation can be the result of:
options: Her request and an agreed non-monetary settlement
questions.why: Conciliation happens at her request and ends in an agreed non-monetary settlement (Section 10).

questions.q: Inquiry completion deadline:
questions.why: The inquiry must be completed within 90 days.

questions.q: Employer acts on the report within:
questions.why: The employer must act on the report within 60 days.

questions.q: Which is valid interim relief?
options: Respondent restrained from writing her appraisal
questions.why: Restraining the respondent from writing her appraisal is valid interim relief under Section 12. Cutting her salary or firing the respondent before the inquiry isn't.

questions.q: Incidents on 10 Jan and 15 March; she files on 1 June. Is it in time without extension?
options: Yes — within 3 months of the last incident (15 March)
questions.why: For a series of incidents, the 3 months run from the last incident, 15 March, so a 1 June complaint is within time.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The IC can punish a complainant whose complaint was not proved. Reason (R): Mere inability to substantiate is not a ground for action.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: mere inability to substantiate a complaint is not a ground for action against the complainant.

questions.q: Lawyers representing parties during IC hearings:
questions.why: The Rules bar lawyers from representing parties in IC hearings.

questions.q: Standard of proof in IC inquiry:
questions.why: The standard of proof in an IC inquiry is the preponderance of probabilities, the civil standard.

questions.q: Case: Complaint received 1 March. The IC finishes hearings on 25 May. By when should the report reach the employer?
questions.why: The report must reach the employer within 10 days of completing the inquiry. Hearings ending 25 May means by 4 June.

questions.q: Case: The respondent has resigned before compensation could be deducted from salary. What can happen?
options: He may be directed to pay; if he fails, recovery as arrears of land revenue via the District Officer
questions.why: If compensation can't be deducted from salary, the respondent may be directed to pay, and the District Officer can recover it as arrears of land revenue.

questions.q: Which Section 15 factor would justify paying compensation in instalments?
options: Respondent's income and financial status / feasibility
questions.why: The respondent's income and financial status decides feasibility, so it can justify instalments. The other factors relate to the complainant's loss.

questions.q: Case: After a settlement (written apology, no contact), the respondent resumes sexual messages. The complainant should:
options: File a fresh complaint after 1 year
Inform the IC, which proceeds with an inquiry
Accept it since it was settled
questions.why: If the respondent resumes harassment after a settlement, the complainant should inform the IC, which proceeds with an inquiry. Non-compliance revives it.

questions.q: A party is absent for three consecutive hearings without cause after notice. The IC may:
options: Terminate or proceed ex parte after 15 days' written notice
questions.why: If a party is absent for three consecutive hearings without cause, the IC may terminate the inquiry or proceed ex parte after 15 days' written notice.

questions.q: Which combination is fully correct about confidentiality?
options: The press may report the report
Identities can be published once the case is closed
Identities and proceedings must not be published; information on justice secured may be shared without identities
Only the respondent's name may be published
questions.why: Section 16 bars publishing identities and proceedings, though information on the justice secured may be shared without identities.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Bystanders, managers and a respectful culture
courses.summary: What a bystander can do, how a manager should respond when someone discloses, handling online harassment and evidence, and looking after yourself.
outcomes: Learners can apply the 5D bystander methods
Learners can respond to a disclosure without blame or delay
Learners can preserve digital evidence safely
Learners know support options and help numbers in India

scenes.text: At a team dinner, a senior keeps putting his arm around a new joiner, Isha. She looks uncomfortable.
Karan notices. He's junior too and doesn't want trouble.
He remembers there are safe ways to step in.

steps.title: The 5Ds
steps.body:
- **Direct:** calmly name it — 'That's not okay, please stop.' (only if safe)
- **Distract:** interrupt — 'Isha, can you help me with the bill?'
- **Delegate:** get help — a manager, IC member, venue staff.
- **Delay:** check in afterwards — 'Are you okay? Want me to come with you to the IC?'
- **Document:** note date, time, what you saw; share **only with her consent**.

steps.title: Solved example: choose the D
steps.body:
**Karan's situation:** junior, senior harasser, public dinner.
**Step 1:** Direct may be risky for him → choose **Distract** now: call Isha to come and see something.
**Step 2:** **Delay:** next day, ask how she is and share the IC's contacts.
**Step 3:** **Document:** write down what he saw in case she decides to complain and needs a witness.

steps.title: Witnesses matter
steps.body: A witness can give evidence to the IC. The Act protects confidentiality of witnesses too, and retaliation against anyone for participating is misconduct under good policies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Filming and posting the incident online — breaches her privacy.
- Confronting the harasser aggressively — may escalate and endanger you.
- Telling her what she *must* do — offer options; the decision is hers.

activity.prompt: Match each action to its D.
pairs: 'Hey, your cab is here!' to pull her away
Telling the event organiser or an IC member
Messaging her the next day to check in
Writing down what you saw, with time and place

quiz.q: Which D is safest when confronting would be risky?
quiz.why: Distract is the safest of the 5Ds when confronting would be risky, because it interrupts the situation without confrontation.

options: Only with the affected person's consent
quiz.why: Documentation should be shared only with the affected person's consent, since it is her choice.

quiz.q: A witness's identity under the Act is:
quiz.why: A witness's identity is confidential under Section 16.
The best bystander attitude is to offer support and options, respecting her agency.
In the 5Ds, Delay means checking in after the incident, to offer support.

lessons.title: When someone tells you: the manager's role

scenes.text: Pooja asks her manager Sameer for 'five minutes'. She says a colleague has been touching her shoulder and making comments.
Sameer's instinct is to say, 'Are you sure? He's a nice guy.'
He stops and remembers his training.

steps.title: LISTEN well
steps.body:
- **Listen** without interrupting; thank her for telling you.
- **Believe** enough to take it seriously — you are not the judge.
- **Don't blame** ('why didn't you tell earlier?', 'what were you wearing?').
- **Explain options:** IC complaint, conciliation (her choice), interim relief, police if she wishes.
- **Act:** share the IC contact; if she agrees, help her reach the IC; take immediate safety steps such as changing seating or meetings.
- **Keep it confidential** — need-to-know only.

steps.title: Solved example: a good reply
steps.body:
**Pooja:** 'He keeps touching my shoulder and saying things about my figure.'
**Sameer:** 'Thank you for trusting me. That's not acceptable. You can go to the Internal Committee — here are the Presiding Officer's details. I can walk with you if you'd like. Meanwhile, would it help if you sat with the design team this week? I won't discuss this with anyone except as needed to help you.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Investigating yourself, or calling the accused in 'to sort it out'.
- Promising total secrecy if policy requires you to report — say 'I'll keep it as confidential as possible.'
- Retaliating: changing her role, rating or shifts negatively after she complains.
- Delaying until 'after the release'.

steps.title: Retaliation is a red line
steps.body: Any adverse action against a complainant or witness for raising a concern undermines the law's purpose and is treated as serious misconduct in good policies.

a.text: Your team member tells you a senior from another team sent her sexual messages. What's your first response?

choices.label: 'Are you sure you didn't misread it?'
'Thank you for telling me. Let's talk about your options, including the IC.'

b.text: She goes quiet and says 'Forget it.' You realise your reply shut her down. Try again?

c.text: She wants to think about it. What do you do next?

choices.feedback: This could tip him off and breach confidentiality.

choices.label: Give her the IC contact, offer interim seating/meeting changes, check in in two days
choices.feedback: Right balance of support and respect.

d.text: The senior deletes the messages and confronts her. Contacting him was a serious mistake. Lesson: never approach the respondent yourself.

e.text: She files a complaint the next week with her saved messages. You cooperated with the IC when asked. Well handled.

quiz.q: When a team member discloses harassment, a manager should first:
quiz.why: When a team member discloses harassment, a manager should first listen and take it seriously. Don't blame or investigate personally.

options: A mistake — it can tip off and pressure
quiz.why: Calling the accused to 'sort it out' is a mistake, because it can tip him off and pressure the complainant. Leave the process to the IC.

options: Offering a seat change she asked for
Giving her a lower rating because she complained
quiz.why: Giving her a lower rating because she complained is retaliation, an adverse action for complaining.
A manager's confidentiality means sharing on a need-to-know basis only.

quiz.why: The decision to file a complaint is the aggrieved woman's. You support her.

Her friend says, 'Screenshot everything right now, with the time and his number visible.'
Tanvi starts a simple evidence log.

steps.title: What online harassment looks like
steps.body: Sexual messages, images or GIFs; comments on photos; repeated unwanted calls or video calls; sexual remarks in meetings or chats; morphing or sharing images; creating fake profiles. If it arises out of work, it falls within the workplace concept.

steps.title: Preserve evidence
steps.body:
- Take **screenshots** showing sender name/number, date and time.
- **Export chats** where the app allows; save emails in original form.
- Keep a **log**: date, time, platform, what happened, who saw.
- Don't edit or crop in a way that removes context.
- Back up to a safe place only you control.

steps.title: Solved example: an evidence log
steps.body:
| Date | Time | Platform | What | Witness |
- 3 Mar · 22:14 · Chat app · Sexual image from R.K. · none
- 5 Mar · 11:02 · Team call · Remark about my body · A.S., M.D.
- 7 Mar · 23:40 · Calls · 4 missed calls from R.K. · screenshot
**Use:** attach to the IC complaint with names of witnesses.

steps.title: Beyond the IC
steps.body: Sharing or threatening to share intimate images, stalking and cyber offences are crimes. In India you can report cybercrime at the national portal **cybercrime.gov.in** or call **1930**; for emergencies call **112**; women's helpline **181**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forwarding explicit images to friends 'as proof' — spreads the harm; give evidence only to the IC/police.
- Deleting the chat out of anger before saving.

lessons.title: Looking after yourself and getting support

scenes.text: After filing, Sana can't sleep and dreads coming to work.
A friend reminds her it's normal to feel this way and that help exists.
She uses the company's counselling line and keeps a routine.

steps.title: Normal reactions
steps.body: Fear, anger, shame, self-doubt, poor sleep, trouble concentrating — these are common responses to harassment. **It is not your fault.**

steps.title: Practical self-care
steps.body:
- Talk to someone you trust.
- Use an Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) or counsellor if available.
- Ask the IC for interim relief if working near the respondent is hard.
- Keep basic routines: sleep, food, movement.
- Try slow breathing when anxious.

steps.title: Help numbers (India)
steps.body:
- **112** — all emergencies
- **181** — women's helpline
- **1930** — cybercrime
- **14416** — Tele-MANAS mental health support

If you feel unsafe or overwhelmed, please reach out now.

steps.title: Solved example: a support plan
steps.body:
**Step 1:** Tell one trusted person.
**Step 2:** Request interim relief (e.g. he doesn't write my appraisal).
**Step 3:** Book two EAP sessions.
**Step 4:** Keep the evidence log updated.
**Step 5:** Plan a calming activity after each hearing.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: If distress lasts weeks, affects sleep or work badly, or you have thoughts of self-harm, see a mental-health professional or call 14416. This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

activity.label: Slow breathing before a hard conversation
