questions.q: Assertion (A): A manager should contact the respondent to hear his side first. Reason (R): Fact-finding belongs to the IC.
questions.why: The assertion is false and the reason is true: fact-finding belongs to the IC, so a manager shouldn't contact the respondent first.

questions.q: A bystander films the incident and posts it online. This:
options: Harms privacy and may breach confidentiality
questions.why: Filming and posting online harms privacy and may breach confidentiality. Document privately and share with consent.

questions.q: Which help number is for mental-health support?
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, 14416, is the mental-health support helpline.

questions.q: Case: A junior sees a VP making sexual comments to an intern at an offsite. Direct action feels unsafe. Best combination?
options: Distract now, check in later, and offer to be a witness
questions.why: When direct action feels unsafe, distract now, check in later and offer to be a witness. Posting on LinkedIn or doing nothing doesn't help.

questions.q: Case: She says 'Please don't tell anyone.' The manager's policy requires reporting to HR/IC. Best reply?
options: 'I'll keep this as confidential as possible and share only what's needed to protect you.'
questions.why: Be honest about limits: promise to keep it as confidential as possible and share only what's needed to protect her. Promising total secrecy may break policy.

questions.q: Case: Disappearing messages are being used. Best immediate step?
options: Screenshot immediately with sender and time visible and log it
questions.why: With disappearing messages, screenshot immediately with sender and time visible and log it. Evidence may vanish if you wait.

questions.q: A complainant's performance drops during inquiry because of stress. The manager should:
options: Consider support and avoid adverse action that may appear retaliatory; seek IC guidance on interim relief
Put her on a PIP immediately
questions.why: Support her and avoid adverse action that may look like retaliation. Seek IC guidance on interim relief.

questions.q: Which response best combines support, process and confidentiality?
options: 'Thank you for telling me; here is the IC contact; I can help with seating changes; I'll share only what's needed.'
questions.why: A supportive, process-aware, confidential reply thanks her, gives the IC contact, offers practical help and shares only what is needed.

courses.title: POSH · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: All key numbers and rules on one sheet, a drill on tricky cases, and a full mock test.
outcomes: Learners can recall every key number in the Act
Learners can apply the Act to mixed scenarios
Learners can score 80%+ on a full mock test

story.title: The night before the compliance quiz

scenes.text: Aditya, a new IC member, wants every number on one page.
He builds a revision sheet and tests himself with flashcards.

steps.title: Numbers to remember
steps.body:
- **10** employees → IC mandatory
- **≥ ½** IC members women; **senior woman** presides; **1 external** member
- **3 years** maximum IC term
- **3 months** to complain (+ **3 months** extension)
- **7 working days** → copy to respondent; **10 working days** → reply
- **90 days** → complete inquiry
- **10 days** → report to employer
- **60 days** → employer acts
- **90 days** → appeal
- **3 months** → interim leave
- **₹50,000** → employer fine (double for repeat + licence risk)

steps.title: Sections at a glance
steps.body:
- S.2 definitions (aggrieved woman, employee, workplace, sexual harassment)
- S.3 prevention & circumstances
- S.4 IC · S.5–8 District Officer & LC
- S.9 complaint · S.10 conciliation · S.11 inquiry · S.12 interim relief
- S.13 report · S.14 false/malicious · S.15 compensation · S.16 confidentiality · S.18 appeal
- S.19 employer duties · S.21 annual report · S.26 penalties

steps.title: Most common exam errors
steps.body:
- Mixing up 90 days (inquiry) and 60 days (employer action).
- Saying conciliation can involve money.
- Saying failure to prove = false complaint.
- Saying IPC is current criminal law — it is the BNS since 1 July 2024.

cards.back: Up to ₹50,000; repeat: double + licence risk

quiz.why: The employer must act on the report within 60 days.
Section 16 of the Act deals with confidentiality.
Section 15 sets out the factors for determining compensation.
The appeal window is 90 days.

scenes.text: The trainer shows six short cases and asks: covered or not, and which committee?
The group checks answers against the Act.

steps.title: Case 1: the vendor
steps.body: A woman from a vendor company is harassed by your employee during a site visit. **Covered** — any woman at your workplace; your IC handles it (and her employer may also help).

steps.title: Case 2: the WhatsApp group
steps.body: Sexual memes in an unofficial team group used to coordinate work. **Likely covered** — conduct arising out of work; policies usually include such groups.

steps.title: Case 3: the owner
steps.body: A 60-person firm's proprietor is the respondent. **Local Committee**.

steps.title: Case 4: the late complaint
steps.body: Filed 5 months after the last incident because she was hospitalised. **IC may extend** (up to 3 more months) recording reasons.

steps.title: Method for any case
steps.body: 1) Is it sexual and unwelcome? 2) Is the place/situation work-linked? 3) Is she an aggrieved woman? 4) Which committee? 5) Time limit? 6) Interim needs?

activity.prompt: Which committee?

items.text: Complaint against the company's own proprietor
Harassment by a stranger at a park on a holiday
Team lead's sexual remarks in a 200-person firm
Domestic worker against householder
Intern harassed at a client site

quiz.q: First question in the case method:
quiz.why: The first question in the case method is whether the conduct is sexual and unwelcome, starting from the definition.

quiz.q: Complaint 5 months late due to hospitalisation:
options: May be admitted with a reasoned extension
quiz.why: A complaint 5 months late due to hospitalisation may be admitted with a reasoned extension of up to 3 more months.

quiz.q: Harassment by a stranger in a park on a holiday:
quiz.why: Harassment by a stranger in a park on a holiday isn't work-linked, so it isn't POSH. Criminal law applies.

quiz.q: A vendor's employee harassed at your office:
quiz.why: A vendor's employee harassed at your office is protected, as the Act covers any woman at the workplace, so your IC can act.

scenes.text: Set a 20-minute timer and attempt the course exam as a mock paper.
Review every 'why' — that's where the learning is.

steps.title: How to use the mock
steps.body: Answer all questions without notes, then review. Aim for **80%+**. Re-read the chapter for any section where you miss two or more.

steps.title: Assertion–reason technique
steps.body: Check A alone (true/false), then R alone, then ask 'does R explain A?' Only then pick the option.

steps.title: Reminder
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Company policies may give more protection than the Act.

activity.prompt: Which part of POSH would you find hardest to apply in real life, and what will you do to prepare?
activity.hint: E.g. responding to a disclosure, intervening as a bystander, timelines.

quiz.why: In assertion–reason questions, first check whether A is true, then evaluate R and whether it explains A.
Aim for a high mock score, 80% or more.

quiz.q: Can a company policy give more protection than the Act?
quiz.why: Yes. A company policy can give more protection than the Act, for example by covering all genders.

questions.q: POSH Act year:
questions.why: The POSH Act is from 2013.

questions.q: Which is sexual harassment under the Act?
questions.why: Sexually coloured remarks are listed as sexual harassment. Fair criticism, deadlines and work assignments are not.

questions.q: Women in IC must be at least:
questions.why: At least one-half of the IC's members must be women.

questions.q: IC is required at:
questions.why: An IC is required where there are 10 or more employees.

questions.q: Complaint time limit:
questions.why: The complaint time limit is 3 months.

questions.q: Conciliation basis cannot be:
questions.why: Money can't be the basis of conciliation. Apology, training and no-contact undertakings can.

questions.q: Inquiry deadline:
questions.why: The inquiry deadline is 90 days.

questions.q: Who constitutes the LC?
questions.why: The District Officer constitutes the Local Committee.

questions.q: Employer-provided cab during work travel is:
questions.why: An employer-provided cab during work travel is expressly included in the workplace.

questions.q: Lawyers in IC proceedings:
questions.why: Lawyers are not allowed in IC proceedings, under the Rules.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A woman need not be an employee to complain. Reason (R): 'Aggrieved woman' includes women employed or not.
options: A and R true, R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: 'aggrieved woman' includes women employed or not, so she need not be an employee to complain.

questions.q: Employer fine for first contravention:
questions.why: An employer's fine for a first contravention is up to ₹50,000 (Section 26).

questions.q: Inability to prove a complaint:
options: Is not by itself grounds for action
questions.why: Inability to prove a complaint isn't by itself grounds for action against the complainant (Section 14 proviso).

questions.q: Case: Last incident 1 Feb; complaint 15 June citing fear of retaliation. IC may:
options: Extend the limit (up to 3 more months) recording reasons
questions.why: The last incident was 1 Feb, so 3 months ended in May, and 15 June is within the extension of up to 3 more months. The IC may extend it, recording its reasons.

questions.q: Case: The respondent is the complainant's appraiser. Which interim relief fits best?
options: Restrain him from assessing her performance
questions.why: When the respondent is the complainant's appraiser, restraining him from assessing her performance is a fitting interim relief under Section 12.

questions.q: Case: The IC finished on 10 May. The report reaches the employer on 30 May. This is:
questions.why: The report should reach the employer within 10 days of the inquiry ending. 10 May to 30 May is 20 days, so it is late.

questions.q: Compensation factor NOT in Section 15:
questions.why: Marital status is not a Section 15 compensation factor. Mental trauma, medical expenses and loss of career opportunity are.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: The inquiry deadline is 90 days and the employer's action deadline is 60 days. This is a commonly confused pair.

questions.q: Case: A company with 9 employees and the owner as respondent. Where to complain?
questions.why: With 9 employees (fewer than 10) and the owner as respondent, the complaint goes to the Local Committee.

questions.q: Best description of the Act's approach:
options: A civil, workplace-based prevention and redressal system that coexists with criminal law (BNS)
questions.why: The Act is a civil, workplace-based prevention and redressal system that coexists with criminal law (BNS). It isn't purely criminal or limited to training.

corp-sysdesign.title: System design for working engineers
corp-sysdesign.description: Chapter-by-chapter system design: requirements and estimation, scaling, caching, databases, queues and streams, and full case studies — with runnable mini-programs and interview-style practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Requirements, estimation, latency and APIs
courses.summary: How to start any design: functional and non-functional requirements, back-of-the-envelope maths, latency and availability numbers, and clean API design.
outcomes: Learners can separate functional from non-functional requirements
Learners can estimate QPS, storage and bandwidth
Learners can convert availability 'nines' into downtime and combine component availability
Learners can design REST APIs with pagination, idempotency and correct status codes

scenes.text: In an interview, Kabir is asked to 'design a photo-sharing app' and starts drawing databases straight away.
The interviewer stops him: 'What exactly are we building, for whom, and how big?'
Kabir learns the first five minutes decide the whole design.

steps.title: Functional requirements
steps.body: What the system **does**: features and use cases. e.g. upload photo, follow users, view feed, like and comment. Narrow scope explicitly: 'We'll skip stories, DMs and search.'

steps.title: Non-functional requirements
steps.body: How well it does it: **scale** (users, requests), **latency** (feed in < 200 ms at p99), **availability** (99.9%+), **consistency** needs (is a slightly stale like-count okay?), **durability** (never lose photos), **security/privacy**, **cost**.

steps.title: Solved example: requirements for a URL shortener
steps.body:
**Functional:** create short URL from long URL; redirect short → long; optional custom alias and expiry.
**Non-functional:** 100M new URLs/month; reads ≫ writes (≈100:1); redirect latency < 50 ms; highly available; short codes must not collide; links durable for years.

steps.title: Solved example: consistency choice
steps.body:
**Feed likes count:** eventual consistency is fine — users accept a count that lags a few seconds.
**Bank balance:** strong consistency required — a stale read can cause double spending.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Jumping to technology (Kafka! Cassandra!) before requirements.
- Ignoring read/write ratio — it drives caching and database choices.
- Not stating assumptions out loud.

activity.prompt: Functional or non-functional?

items.text: Users can upload a profile photo
p99 latency under 200 ms
Users can follow other users
99.95% availability
Data encrypted at rest
Users can delete a comment

quiz.why: 'Feed loads in under 200 ms' is a quality target, so it is a non-functional requirement. Functional requirements describe what the system does.

options: It drives caching and storage choices
quiz.why: The read/write ratio drives caching and storage choices: read-heavy systems benefit from caches and replicas.
A bank balance needs strong consistency because money must be correct. View, like and trending counts can be approximate.

quiz.q: First step in a design interview:
quiz.why: The first step is to clarify requirements and scope, before drawing or coding.
Durability means data isn't lost once it is written.

scenes.text: Product says: '10 million daily users, 10 actions each.' The architect asks Ishita: 'What's our QPS?'
She uses one trick: a day has about 86,400 seconds — call it 10⁵.

steps.title: Handy numbers
steps.body:
- 1 day = 86,400 s ≈ **10⁵ s**
- 1 month ≈ 2.6 × 10⁶ s
- 1 KB = 10³ B, 1 MB = 10⁶ B, 1 GB = 10⁹ B, 1 TB = 10¹² B, 1 PB = 10¹⁵ B (decimal approximations)
- Peak traffic ≈ **2–3×** average (state your assumption)

steps.title: Solved example 1: QPS
steps.body:
10M DAU × 10 requests = 10⁸ requests/day.
**Average QPS** = 10⁸ / 86,400 ≈ **1,157** (≈ 1,200).
**Peak** (×2) ≈ **2,300 QPS**.
If one app server handles ~500 QPS comfortably → ~5 servers at peak, plus headroom and redundancy → 8.

steps.title: Solved example 2: storage
steps.body:
Photo app: 1M uploads/day × 2 MB = 2 TB/day.
Per year: 2 TB × 365 ≈ **730 TB**. With 3 replicas ≈ **2.2 PB/year**. Conclusion: object storage, not a relational DB, for image bytes; DB stores metadata only.

steps.title: Solved example 3: bandwidth
steps.body: Peak 2,300 QPS × 50 KB average response = 115,000 KB/s ≈ **115 MB/s ≈ 0.92 Gbps** egress → a CDN is worth considering.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Precision obsession — round aggressively and keep going.
- Forgetting replication factor in storage.
- Mixing bits and bytes (1 byte = 8 bits).

activity.prompt: Read DAU and requests per user per day from one line. Print average QPS (integer division by 86400) and peak QPS (= 2 × average), separated by a space.
activity.starter:
dau, rpu = map(int, input().split())
# total requests per day
# avg = ...
# peak = ...
print(avg, peak)
activity.solution:
dau, rpu = map(int, input().split())
total = dau * rpu
avg = total // 86400
peak = avg * 2
print(avg, peak)

quiz.why: A day has 24 × 3,600 = 86,400 seconds, about 10⁵.
10⁸ requests ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 1,160 requests per second.

quiz.q: 2 TB/day for a year with 3 replicas ≈
quiz.why: 2 TB/day × 365 = 730 TB, and with 3 replicas that is about 2,190 TB, roughly 2.2 PB.

quiz.q: Peak traffic is usually assumed to be:
quiz.why: Peak traffic is commonly assumed to be 2 to 3 times the average.
115 MB/s × 8 bits per byte = 920 Mb/s, about 0.92 Gbps.

scenes.text: Dashboards show average latency of 80 ms. Users still complain the app is slow.
SRE Mehul checks p99: 2.4 seconds. One in a hundred requests is painful.

steps.title: Latency orders of magnitude (rough)
steps.body:
- Memory reference: ~100 ns
- Read 1 MB sequentially from memory: ~microseconds
- SSD random read: ~tens to 100+ µs
- Round trip within a data centre: ~0.5 ms
- Disk seek (HDD): ~ms
- Round trip across continents: ~100–150 ms
Lesson: **memory ≫ SSD ≫ network ≫ disk seek ≫ cross-continent** in speed — cache in memory and keep data close to users.

steps.title: Percentiles
steps.body: **p50** (median) = half of requests are faster. **p99** = 99% are faster; the slowest 1% are slower. Users who make many requests hit the tail often, so design and SLOs usually target **p95/p99**, not averages.

steps.title: Nines of availability
steps.body:
Downtime per year (365 days = 8,760 h):
- 99% → 87.6 hours
- 99.9% → 8.76 hours
- 99.99% → ~52.6 minutes
- 99.999% → ~5.26 minutes

steps.title: Solved example: components in series and parallel
steps.body:
**Series** (request needs both A and B): A = 99.9%, B = 99.9% → 0.999 × 0.999 = **99.8%** (worse than each).
**Parallel** (two redundant copies, either works): each 99% → 1 − (0.01 × 0.01) = **99.99%**.
So redundancy raises availability; long dependency chains lower it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reporting averages only.
- Assuming adding services keeps availability the same — series dependencies multiply.
- Forgetting planned maintenance counts against availability unless excluded in the SLA.

activity.prompt: Three services in series, each 99.9% available. Overall availability (in %, two decimals)?

quiz.q: 99.9% availability allows about how much downtime per year?
quiz.why: 99.9% availability allows 0.1% downtime: 0.001 × 8,760 hours ≈ 8.76 hours a year.

options: The value 99% of requests are faster than
quiz.why: p99 latency is the value that 99% of requests are faster than. It shows the slow tail.
Two 99% replicas in parallel fail only if both fail: 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 99.99%.
A memory reference takes nanoseconds, far faster than an SSD read, HDD seek or cross-continent round trip.

quiz.q: Two 99.9% services in series give about:
quiz.why: Services in series multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, which is 99.8%.

scenes.text: A user taps 'Pay' on a flaky network. The app retries. The customer is charged twice.
The fix: an idempotency key so retries don't repeat the charge.

steps.title: REST basics
steps.body:
Resources as nouns, HTTP verbs as actions:
- `GET /users/42` read
- `POST /orders` create
- `PUT /users/42` replace (idempotent)
- `PATCH /users/42` partial update
- `DELETE /orders/9` delete (idempotent)
**Idempotent** = doing it twice has the same effect as once. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent by design; POST is not.

steps.title: Status codes to know
steps.body: 200 OK · 201 Created · 204 No Content · 400 Bad Request · 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated) · 403 Forbidden (authenticated, not allowed) · 404 Not Found · 409 Conflict · 429 Too Many Requests · 500 Internal Server Error · 503 Service Unavailable

steps.title: Solved example: idempotent payments
steps.body:
Client generates `Idempotency-Key: 7f3a...` and sends `POST /payments`.
**Server:** if key unseen → process, store (key → result). If seen → return stored result without charging again.
**Result:** retries are safe.

steps.title: Solved example: pagination
steps.body:
**Offset:** `GET /posts?limit=20&offset=40` — simple, but slow on deep pages and can skip/duplicate items when new posts arrive.
**Cursor:** `GET /posts?limit=20&after=post_981` — stable and fast with an index on the sort key. Prefer cursor for feeds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Verbs in URLs (`/getUser`).
- Returning 200 with an error message in the body.
- Confusing 401 and 403.
- No versioning (`/v1/`) for public APIs.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the status code.

quiz.q: Which method is NOT idempotent by default?
quiz.why: POST isn't idempotent by default, as each call can create a new resource. PUT, DELETE and GET are idempotent.
An idempotency key prevents duplicate processing on retries, because the server recognises a repeated request.

quiz.q: Cursor pagination is better for feeds because:
options: Stable and efficient as data changes
quiz.why: Cursor pagination is better for feeds because it stays stable and efficient as data changes, with no skips or duplicates.
403 means Forbidden: the caller is authenticated but not permitted.
429 means Too Many Requests, used for rate limiting.

questions.q: Non-functional requirement example:
questions.why: 99.9% availability is a quality attribute, so it is non-functional. Follow, delete and upload describe functions.

questions.q: Seconds per day:
questions.why: A day has 24 × 3,600 = 86,400 seconds.

questions.q: 201 status means:
questions.why: HTTP 201 means Created.

questions.q: Idempotent method:
questions.why: PUT is idempotent: repeating it gives the same result. POST is not.

questions.q: 99.99% availability ≈ downtime per year:
questions.why: 99.99% availability allows 0.01% downtime: 0.0001 × 525,600 minutes ≈ 52.6 minutes a year.

questions.q: Why prefer p99 over average?
options: Captures tail experienced by many users
questions.why: p99 captures the tail latency that many users experience, while the average hides slow requests.

questions.q: 50M requests/day ≈ average QPS:
questions.why: 50M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 579, so about 580 requests per second.

questions.q: Two 99.9% services in series ≈
questions.why: Two services in series multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.8%.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Offset pagination can show duplicates when new items arrive. Reason (R): Offsets shift as rows are inserted ahead.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A: with offset pagination, new rows inserted ahead shift the offsets, so items can repeat.

questions.q: Storage for 500K uploads/day × 4 MB for 1 year, no replication ≈
questions.why: 500K × 4 MB = 2 TB a day, and 2 TB × 365 = 730 TB for a year.

questions.q: Case: A mobile app retries POST /orders on timeout and creates duplicates. Best fix?
questions.why: A client-generated idempotency key, stored server-side, lets the server recognise a retried POST and return the original result. This makes retries safe, instead of creating duplicate orders.

questions.q: Case: 2 redundant load balancers at 99.5% each (parallel), then an app tier at 99.9% (series). Overall ≈
questions.why: The pair of 99.5% load balancers in parallel fails only if both fail: 1 − 0.005² = 99.9975%. In series with the 99.9% app tier: 0.999975 × 0.999 ≈ 99.897%, about 99.9%.

questions.q: Peak 3,000 QPS × 20 KB responses ≈ egress:
questions.why: 3,000 QPS × 20 KB = 60,000 KB/s = 60 MB/s. Multiplying by 8 bits per byte gives about 480 Mbps.

questions.q: Which is the strongest reason to version public APIs (/v1/)?
questions.why: Versioning public APIs (such as /v1/) lets you evolve them without breaking existing clients.

questions.q: Case: A dependency chain of 10 services each 99.9% in series. Overall ≈
questions.why: Ten services in series multiply: 0.999¹⁰ ≈ 0.990, about 99.0%. Each dependency lowers overall availability.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Scaling services and load balancing
courses.summary: Vertical vs horizontal scaling, stateless services and sessions, load balancers and algorithms, health checks, autoscaling, and why consistent hashing exists.
outcomes: Learners can choose between vertical and horizontal scaling
Learners can make services stateless
Learners can compare load-balancing algorithms and L4 vs L7
Learners can explain consistent hashing and why modulo hashing reshuffles keys

story.title: The biggest server we could buy

scenes.text: A ticketing startup keeps upgrading to bigger machines before every concert sale.
At the largest size, one crash takes the whole site down.
They redesign to many small, stateless servers.

steps.title: Vertical scaling (scale up)
steps.body: Bigger machine: more CPU, RAM, faster disk. **Pros:** simple, no code change. **Cons:** hardware ceiling, cost rises steeply, single point of failure, downtime to resize.

steps.title: Horizontal scaling (scale out)
steps.body: More machines behind a load balancer. **Pros:** near-linear capacity, fault tolerance, autoscaling. **Cons:** requires **stateless** design, distributed-systems complexity (consistency, coordination).

steps.title: Making services stateless
steps.body: Don't keep user session data in server memory. Store sessions in a shared store (Redis), use signed tokens (JWT) carried by clients, put files in object storage. Then **any** server can handle **any** request.

steps.title: Solved example: sticky sessions problem
steps.body:
**Setup:** sessions in server memory + load balancer with sticky sessions.
**Failure:** server 3 dies → its users are logged out and lose carts.
**Fix:** move sessions to Redis (replicated) → servers become interchangeable; sticky sessions no longer needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Scaling the app tier while the single database becomes the bottleneck.
- Writing uploads to local disk on app servers.
- Assuming horizontal scaling is always cheaper — start simple, scale when data says so.

activity.prompt: Vertical or horizontal?

items.text: Upgrade from 16 GB to 128 GB RAM
Add 10 more app servers behind a load balancer
Autoscale container replicas from 3 to 30
Move to a CPU with more cores on the same box
Add read replicas to spread reads

quiz.q: Main prerequisite for horizontal scaling of app servers:
quiz.why: Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, so any server can handle any request. Sticky sessions tie users to specific servers.

options: Hardware ceiling and single point of failure
quiz.why: Vertical scaling has a hardware ceiling and leaves a single point of failure, since you rely on one big machine.

quiz.q: Where should sessions live for stateless apps?
options: Shared store like Redis or signed tokens
quiz.why: For stateless apps, keep sessions in a shared store like Redis or in signed tokens. Local files or server RAM tie them to one server.
Uploaded files should go to object storage, which is shared and durable. App server local disks are lost or unavailable to other servers.
Horizontal scaling improves both capacity and fault tolerance, since more machines handle more load and one failure matters less.

scenes.text: With round-robin, one server handling slow video uploads is at 100% CPU while others idle.
Switching to least-connections spreads the load better.

steps.title: L4 vs L7
steps.body:
- **Layer 4 (transport):** routes by IP/port (TCP/UDP); very fast; can't see URLs or headers.
- **Layer 7 (application):** understands HTTP — route by path (`/api` vs `/images`), headers, cookies; can terminate TLS, rewrite, rate-limit.

steps.title: Algorithms
steps.body:
- **Round robin:** next server in turn — simple, assumes equal requests.
- **Weighted round robin:** bigger servers get more.
- **Least connections:** to the server with fewest active connections — good for uneven request durations.
- **IP/consistent hash:** same client/key → same server (affinity, caches).
- **Random with two choices:** pick two at random, send to the less loaded — simple and effective.

steps.title: Health checks
steps.body: The load balancer probes each server (e.g. `GET /health` every 10 s). Failing servers are removed until healthy. Use **readiness** (can take traffic?) vs **liveness** (is it alive?) checks in container platforms.

steps.title: Solved example: round robin by hand
steps.body:
Servers A, B, C; 7 requests → A, B, C, A, B, C, A.
**Request k** (0-based) goes to server `k mod 3`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A single load balancer as a new single point of failure — run it redundantly (managed LBs do this).
- Health checks that only test 'process alive' while the DB connection is broken.

activity.prompt: Round-robin: line 1 has server names separated by spaces; line 2 has N (number of requests). Print the server chosen for each request, space-separated.
activity.starter:
servers = input().split()
n = int(input())
# choose server for each request k = 0..n-1
activity.solution:
servers = input().split()
n = int(input())
print(' '.join(servers[k % len(servers)] for k in range(n)))

quiz.why: Routing /images and /api to different pools needs a Layer 7 load balancer, because it understands HTTP paths. Layer 4 sees only IPs and ports.

steps.title: The modulo problem
steps.body: With `hash(key) % N`, changing N changes the mapping for **most** keys. Going from N to N+1 moves roughly **N/(N+1)** of keys — e.g. ~80% when going 4 → 5.

steps.title: The ring
steps.body: **Consistent hashing** places both servers and keys on a hash ring (0 … 2³²−1). Each key belongs to the **next server clockwise**. Adding a server only takes keys from its clockwise neighbour → only about **1/N** of keys move.

steps.title: Virtual nodes
steps.body: Each physical server is placed at many points (e.g. 100–200 virtual nodes) to spread load evenly and to share the load of a failed server among many others. Used in distributed caches and databases (e.g. Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra).

steps.title: Solved example: count moved keys with modulo

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using modulo hashing for caches that scale up and down.
- Too few virtual nodes → uneven 'hot' servers.

courses.summary: Where to cache, cache patterns, eviction policies with an LRU implementation, invalidation and stampedes, and content delivery networks.

scenes.text: An e-commerce product page makes 12 database queries; at sale time the DB melts.
Adding a Redis cache cuts DB load by 90%.

steps.title: Cache layers
steps.body: Browser cache → CDN/edge → API gateway/reverse proxy → application in-memory cache → distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) → database buffer cache. Cache as close to the user as correctness allows.

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body:
- **Cache-aside (lazy):** app checks cache; on miss reads DB and fills cache. Most common.
- **Read-through:** cache library loads from DB on miss.
- **Write-through:** write to cache and DB together — cache always fresh, writes slower.
- **Write-back (write-behind):** write to cache, flush to DB later — fast writes, risk of loss if cache fails.
- **Write-around:** write to DB only; cache filled on read.

steps.title: Solved example: hit ratio maths
steps.body:
DB read = 10 ms, cache read = 1 ms, hit ratio 90%.
**Average** = 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × (1 + 10) = 0.9 + 1.1 = **2.0 ms** (miss pays cache check + DB).
DB load drops to 10% of reads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Caching without a TTL — stale forever.
- Caching per-user sensitive data in a shared CDN cache.
- Treating the cache as the source of truth for critical data.

quiz.why: Cache-aside is the most common caching pattern in web apps because it is simple and flexible.

options: Data loss if cache fails before flush
quiz.why: Write-back risks data loss if the cache fails before the data is flushed to the database.

scenes.text: The cache has room for 1 million items, but there are 50 million products.
Which ones should it throw out? The eviction policy decides.

steps.title: Policies
steps.body:
- **LRU** (least recently used): evict the item unused for longest — good default.
- **LFU** (least frequently used): evict the least-used — good for stable popularity.
- **FIFO:** oldest inserted first — simple, often worse.
- **TTL-based:** expire after a time.
Redis supports policies like allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu.

steps.title: Solved example: LRU by hand
steps.body:
Capacity 2; access A, B, A, C, B.
- A: miss → [A]
- B: miss → [A, B]
- A: hit → order [B, A]
- C: miss → evict B (least recent) → [A, C]
- B: miss → evict A → [C, B]
**Result:** hits = 1, misses = 4.

steps.title: How LRU is built
steps.body: A **hash map + doubly linked list** gives O(1) get and put: the map finds nodes; the list keeps recency order (move to front on access, evict from tail). In Python, `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` does the same.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to update recency on a hit.
- O(n) list scans for every access.

activity.prompt: Simulate an LRU cache. Line 1: capacity. Line 2: keys accessed, space-separated. Print 'hits=H misses=M'.

activity.solution:
from collections import OrderedDict
cap = int(input())
keys = input().split()
cache = OrderedDict()
hits = misses = 0
for k in keys:
    if k in cache:
        hits += 1
        cache.move_to_end(k)
    else:
        misses += 1
        cache[k] = True
        if len(cache) > cap:
            cache.popitem(last=False)
print(f'hits={hits} misses={misses}')
activity.hint: On hit: move_to_end. On miss: insert, and if over capacity popitem(last=False).

steps.title: Invalidation strategies
steps.body:
- **TTL expiry:** simple; staleness up to TTL.
- **Delete on write:** after updating DB, delete the cache key (next read refills).
- **Versioned keys:** `product:42:v7` — bump version on change.
- **Event-driven:** DB change events (CDC) invalidate caches.

steps.title: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
steps.body: When a hot key expires, many requests miss simultaneously and hammer the DB. Fixes: **request coalescing/locking** (one request rebuilds, others wait), **early refresh** before expiry, **TTL jitter** (random offsets), serve **stale-while-revalidate**.

steps.title: Solved example: update order
steps.body:
**Wrong:** delete cache, then update DB → a reader in between re-caches the old value.
**Better:** update DB, **then** delete cache. For extra safety, a short TTL limits damage if a race still happens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Same TTL for millions of keys set at the same time → synchronized expiry storms.
- Caching errors/empty results for too long (negative caching needs short TTL).

statements.s: Adding random jitter to TTLs helps avoid synchronized expiry.
Deleting the cache before updating the DB is the safest order.
Request coalescing lets one request rebuild a hot key while others wait.
Stale-while-revalidate serves slightly old data while refreshing in the background.

options: A hot key expires and many requests miss at once
quiz.why: Thundering herd happens when a hot key expires and many requests miss at once, all hitting the database.

Negative caching ('not found') should use a short TTL, so new data isn't hidden for long.

steps.title: What a CDN does
steps.body: A **Content Delivery Network** caches content at many **edge locations** close to users. Benefits: lower latency, less load and egress from your origin, absorption of traffic spikes and some DDoS protection.

steps.title: Controlling caching
steps.body: HTTP headers: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400` (cache 1 day), `private` (browser only), `no-store` (don't cache). Use **content-hashed filenames** (`app.3f9a.js`) for long caching with instant updates. Invalidate (purge) on change when needed.

steps.title: Solved example: what to put on the CDN
steps.body:
✔ Images, videos, JS/CSS bundles, fonts, public downloadable PDFs.
✔ Public API responses that are the same for all users (short TTL).
✘ Personalised pages with account details (unless carefully keyed and marked private).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Caching pages with `Set-Cookie` or user data publicly → data leak.
- Long max-age on non-hashed filenames → users stuck with old files.

scenes.text: A team picks a document DB 'because it scales', then struggles with joins for invoices and payments.
The architect says: choose by access patterns, not hype.

steps.title: Families
steps.body:
- **Relational (SQL):** tables, schemas, joins, ACID transactions — PostgreSQL, MySQL.
- **Key-value:** get/put by key, very fast — Redis, DynamoDB.
- **Document:** JSON-like documents, flexible schema — MongoDB.
- **Wide-column:** rows with many columns, partitioned at scale — Cassandra, HBase.
- **Graph:** nodes and edges — Neo4j.
- **Time-series / search:** metrics stores, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch.

steps.title: Solved example: pick per use case
steps.body:
- Payments, orders, inventory → **SQL** (transactions, constraints).
- Session store, rate-limit counters → **key-value**.
- Product catalogue with varied attributes → **document**.
- IoT sensor readings at huge write rates → **wide-column/time-series**.
- Friend-of-friend recommendations → **graph**.
- Full-text product search → **search engine**.

steps.title: Polyglot persistence
steps.body: Large systems often use several stores, each for what it does best — with one **source of truth** per data item and pipelines to keep others in sync.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'NoSQL scales, SQL doesn't' — modern SQL scales far with replicas, partitioning and good indexing.
- Choosing schemaless and ending with inconsistent data.

quiz.why: A relational DB is the best default for financial transactions because of ACID guarantees.

Choose databases primarily by access patterns and consistency needs, not popularity.

steps.title: B-tree indexes
steps.body: Most relational indexes are **B-trees** (B+ trees): sorted, balanced trees with high fan-out. Lookup costs about **log_f(N)** page reads. With fan-out ~100 and 100M rows: log₁₀₀(10⁸) = **4 levels** — a handful of reads instead of scanning 100M rows.

steps.title: Composite and covering indexes
steps.body: Composite index (a, b) helps queries filtering on **a**, or **a and b** — the leftmost-prefix rule. It does not help a filter on **b** alone. A **covering** index includes all columns the query needs, so the table itself isn't read.

steps.title: Solved example: which index?
steps.body:
Query: `SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`.
**Index:** (user_id, created_at) — equality column first, then range/sort column. Add `total` as an included column to make it covering.

steps.title: The cost of indexes
steps.body: Every index speeds reads but **slows writes** (each insert/update must update indexes) and uses storage. Index for real query patterns; check with `EXPLAIN`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrapping indexed columns in functions (`WHERE LOWER(email)=...`) without a matching expression index.
- Leading wildcard `LIKE '%gmail.com'` can't use a normal B-tree.
- Indexing every column.

steps.title: ACID
steps.body:
- **Atomicity:** all or nothing.
- **Consistency:** constraints hold before and after.
- **Isolation:** concurrent transactions don't interfere improperly.
- **Durability:** committed data survives crashes (write-ahead log).

steps.title: Isolation levels and anomalies
steps.body:
- **Read uncommitted:** dirty reads possible.
- **Read committed:** no dirty reads; non-repeatable reads possible.
- **Repeatable read:** same row reads stay the same; phantoms possible in the SQL standard definition.
- **Serializable:** behaves as if transactions ran one by one.
Anomalies: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update, write skew.

steps.title: Solved example: the last seat
steps.body:
**Fix 1 (pessimistic):** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the seat row; the second transaction waits, then sees it taken.
**Fix 2 (optimistic):** `UPDATE seats SET booked_by=? WHERE id=? AND booked_by IS NULL` — check affected rows = 1; if 0, someone else won.
**Fix 3:** unique constraint on (flight, seat) in bookings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Read-then-write in application code without locks or conditions → lost updates.
- Long transactions holding locks during network calls.

quiz.why: A dirty read means reading uncommitted data.
Serializable is the strongest isolation level, behaving as if transactions ran one after another.
Durability is usually implemented with write-ahead logging (WAL).

options: Rows affected by a conditional UPDATE
quiz.why: Optimistic seat booking checks the rows affected by a conditional UPDATE. If zero rows changed, someone else took the seat.
A lost update happens with an unprotected read-modify-write, where concurrent writes overwrite each other.

scenes.text: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and it's gone. A minute later it's back.
The read went to a replica that hadn't caught up yet: replication lag.

steps.title: Replication
steps.body: **Leader–follower:** writes go to the leader; followers copy changes and serve reads. **Synchronous** replication waits for followers (safer, slower); **asynchronous** doesn't (faster, may lose recent writes on failover, causes lag). **Read-your-writes** fix: route a user's reads to the leader for a short time after they write.

steps.title: CAP and PACELC
steps.body: **CAP:** during a network **P**artition, a distributed system must choose **C**onsistency (refuse/limit some requests) or **A**vailability (answer, maybe stale). **PACELC** adds: **E**lse (no partition), trade **L**atency vs **C**onsistency. e.g. many Dynamo-style stores are PA/EL; traditional single-leader SQL with sync replicas leans PC/EC.

steps.title: Sharding (partitioning)
steps.body:
Split data across machines by a **shard key**:
- **Range** (by date or ID range): good for range scans; risk of hot latest shard.
- **Hash** (hash of user_id): even spread; range queries harder.
- **Directory/lookup:** a map of key → shard; flexible, extra hop.
Good keys have **high cardinality** and spread **load**, and keep related data together (e.g. all of a user's orders).

steps.title: Solved example: pick a shard key
steps.body:
Chat app messages: query 'messages in conversation X, newest first'.
**Key:** conversation_id (hash) → all messages for a conversation on one shard; sort by timestamp inside.
**Avoid:** timestamp as key → all new writes hit one shard (hot spot).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharding too early — try indexes, caching and read replicas first.
- Cross-shard joins and transactions everywhere.
- Celebrity/hot keys overwhelming one shard — add splitting or caching for them.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Queues, streams and asynchronous processing
courses.summary: Why queues decouple systems, delivery guarantees and idempotent consumers, pub/sub and Kafka-style logs, and retries, backoff, dead-letter queues and the outbox pattern.
outcomes: Learners can explain how queues buffer and decouple

scenes.text: Checkout waits for the email service, the invoice PDF and the warehouse API. Any slowness makes checkout fail.
Moving those to a queue makes checkout fast and resilient.

steps.title: Decoupling
steps.body: A **producer** puts messages on a queue; **consumers** process them independently. The producer doesn't wait for or even know the consumers. If a consumer is down, messages wait safely.

steps.title: Buffering spikes
steps.body: Queues absorb bursts: 10,000 orders in a minute can be processed by workers at a steady 2,000/min. Scale workers on **queue depth**.

steps.title: Solved example: checkout redesign
steps.body:
**Synchronous part:** validate cart, charge payment, write order → return 'Order placed'.
**Async via queue (OrderPlaced event):** send email, generate invoice, notify warehouse, update analytics.
**Result:** faster checkout; a failing email service no longer blocks orders.

steps.title: Solved example: drain time
steps.body:
Backlog 120,000 messages; 20 workers × 50 msg/s = 1,000 msg/s.
**Drain time** = 120,000 / 1,000 = **120 s** (if no new arrivals).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the critical payment step on a queue without telling the user it's pending.
- No monitoring of queue age/depth → silent backlogs.

steps.title: Guarantees
steps.body:
- **At-most-once:** ack before processing; may lose messages, never duplicates.
- **At-least-once:** ack after processing; never lose, may **duplicate** (most common).
- **Exactly-once processing:** in practice achieved as **at-least-once + idempotent processing** (or transactional systems that commit output and offsets together).

steps.title: Idempotent consumers
steps.body: Give each message a unique ID. Before processing, check a **processed-IDs** store (or use a unique constraint); skip if seen. Or make the operation naturally idempotent (`SET status='PAID'` rather than `balance = balance - 100`).

**Processed 3, duplicates 2.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the queue guarantees no duplicates.
- Incrementing counters on each delivery.
- Keeping the dedupe store forever with no TTL/size plan.

steps.title: Queue vs pub/sub
steps.body:
- **Queue (point-to-point):** each message is handled by **one** consumer among workers.
- **Pub/sub:** each message goes to **every** subscriber group.
Kafka combines both: **consumer groups** each get all messages; within a group, partitions are split among members.

steps.title: Kafka concepts
steps.body:
- **Topic:** named stream of records.
- **Partition:** ordered, append-only log; ordering is guaranteed **within a partition only**.
- **Key:** records with the same key go to the same partition (e.g. order_id → per-order ordering).
- **Offset:** position of a record; consumers commit offsets.
- **Consumer group:** at most one consumer per partition in a group → max parallelism = number of partitions.
- **Retention:** records kept for a time/size, enabling **replay**.

steps.title: Solved example: parallelism
steps.body: Topic with **6 partitions**; group with **8 consumers** → only 6 are active, 2 idle. To use 8, increase partitions (plan ahead — changing partition count remaps keys).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting global ordering across partitions.
- Random keys when per-entity order matters.
- Too few partitions for future scale.

lessons.title: Retries, backoff, DLQs and the outbox pattern

scenes.text: A partner API slows down; 5,000 workers retry instantly and endlessly.
The partner goes fully down. Backoff with jitter and a dead-letter queue would have prevented it.

steps.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
steps.body: Wait longer after each failure: base × 2^attempt (e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s), capped, plus **random jitter** so clients don't retry in sync. Retry only **transient** errors (timeouts, 503, 429); don't retry 400-type validation errors.

steps.title: Dead-letter queue (DLQ)
steps.body: After N failed attempts, move the message to a **DLQ** for inspection, so one 'poison' message doesn't block or loop forever. Alert on DLQ growth.

steps.title: Transactional outbox
steps.body: Problem: write to DB **and** publish an event — one may succeed and the other fail. **Outbox:** in the same DB transaction, write the business row **and** an 'outbox' row; a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, marking rows sent. Consumers stay idempotent because the relay may publish twice.

steps.title: Solved example: backoff schedule
steps.body: Base 1 s, factor 2, cap 30 s, 6 retries: waits 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 (capped from 32) → total wait ≈ **61 s** before the message goes to the DLQ (plus jitter).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Immediate infinite retries.
- Retrying non-idempotent operations without keys.
- 'Dual writes' to DB and broker without an outbox.

questions.q: Case: Service writes order to DB then publishes event; broker down → order saved, no event. Fix?
questions.why: Use a transactional outbox: write the event with the order in one DB transaction and publish it later. This fixes the dual-write problem.

questions.q: Case: Events for the same account processed out of order. Likely cause and fix?
options: Random partition keys → key by account_id
questions.why: Random partition keys scatter an account's events across partitions, so ordering is lost. Key by account_id to keep them in one partition.

questions.q: Case: One malformed message crashes consumers repeatedly, blocking a partition. Fix?
options: Retry limit then DLQ, with alerting
questions.why: A malformed 'poison' message should be retried a limited number of times, then moved to a DLQ with alerting, so it stops blocking the partition.

questions.why: 7 attempts have 6 waits: 0.5 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 8 (capped at 8) = 23.5 s.

questions.q: Why can't 'exactly-once' be guaranteed by the network alone?
options: A sender can't distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must retry, risking duplicates
questions.why: A sender can't tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must retry and may create duplicates. That is why exactly-once can't be guaranteed by the network alone.

scenes.text: A buggy client script calls the public API 50,000 times a minute.

steps.title: Algorithms
steps.body:
- **Token bucket:** bucket holds up to C tokens, refilled at R/s; each request takes one → allows bursts up to C, average R.
- **Leaky bucket:** requests processed at a fixed rate; smooths bursts.
- **Fixed window counter:** count per minute; simple; burst at window edges.
- **Sliding window log/counter:** more accurate, a bit more cost.

steps.title: Where and how
steps.body: At the API gateway or a middleware layer. Key by API key/user/IP. Store counters in Redis with atomic operations (INCR with expiry, or Lua scripts). Return **429** with a `Retry-After` header; expose limits in headers.

steps.title: Solved example: token bucket trace
steps.body:
C = 2, R = 1/s, bucket full at t=0. Requests at t = 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 3:
- t0: 2→1 ✔, 1→0 ✔, 0 ✘
- t1: +1 → 1 → 0 ✔; next ✘
- t3: +2 → 2 (cap) → 1 ✔
**Result:** A A D A D A

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Non-atomic read-then-write counters → limits exceeded under concurrency.
- Per-server in-memory limits behind a load balancer → effective limit × N servers.
- Fixed windows allowing 2× bursts at the boundary.

activity.prompt: Token bucket. Line 1: capacity C and refill rate R (tokens per second). Line 2: request timestamps (integer seconds, non-decreasing). Bucket starts full at time 0. For each request print A (allowed) or D (denied) with no spaces.
activity.starter:
C, R = map(int, input().split())
ts = list(map(int, input().split()))
tokens, last = C, 0
out = ''
for t in ts:
    pass  # refill, then allow or deny

activity.solution:
C, R = map(int, input().split())
ts = list(map(int, input().split()))
tokens, last = C, 0
out = ''
for t in ts:
    tokens = min(C, tokens + (t - last) * R)
    last = t
    if tokens >= 1:
        tokens -= 1
        out += 'A'
    else:
        out += 'D'
print(out)
activity.hint: tokens = min(C, tokens + (t - last) * R) before each decision.

If we write it into 40 million feeds instantly, the system chokes. If we compute every feed on read, timelines are slow.

steps.title: Fan-out on write (push)
steps.body: When a user posts, write the post ID into each follower's precomputed feed (in Redis/wide-column). **Reads are fast.** Costly for users with huge follower counts.

steps.title: Fan-out on read (pull)
steps.body: Build the feed at read time by fetching recent posts from everyone you follow and merging. **Writes are cheap**; reads are heavier.

steps.title: Hybrid
steps.body: Push for normal users; **pull for celebrities** (their posts merged in at read time). Cache feeds; store only post IDs in feeds and hydrate details from a post cache; rank with a scoring service; paginate with cursors.

steps.title: Solved example: cost of push
steps.body: Average user: 200 followers; 50M posts/day → 10¹⁰ feed inserts/day ≈ **116,000 writes/s** on average. A single 40M-follower post would add 40M writes alone — hence pull for celebrities.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Connections
steps.body: Clients keep a **WebSocket** (or similar long-lived connection) to a **chat gateway**. A presence/session service records which gateway each user is connected to (e.g. in Redis).

steps.title: Send path

steps.title: Groups
steps.body: Small groups: fan-out to each member's connection. Large groups/channels: fan-out via a pub/sub per channel. Media goes to object storage; messages carry links.

scenes.text: Rhea calculates sales commission at 5% in cell B1 and copies her formula down. Every row after the first shows 0.

steps.title: Formulas start with =
steps.body: A formula begins with **=**: `=A2*B1`. Operators: + − * / ^ (power). Excel follows the usual order: brackets, powers, × ÷, + −. `=2+3*4` gives 14; `=(2+3)*4` gives 20.

steps.title: Reference types
steps.body:
- **Relative** `A2`: changes when copied (A2 → A3 when copied down).
- **Absolute** `$B$1`: never changes.
- **Mixed** `$A2` (column fixed) or `A$2` (row fixed).
Press **F4** (Windows) while editing a reference to cycle through types.

steps.title: Solved example: Rhea's fix
steps.body:
Rate in **B1**; sales in A4:A20.
**Wrong:** `=A4*B1` copied down becomes `=A5*B2`, `=A6*B3`… (empty cells → 0).
**Right:** `=A4*$B$1` copied down becomes `=A5*$B$1` ✔.

steps.title: Solved example: a multiplication table with mixed refs
steps.body: Numbers 1–9 in B1:J1 (across) and A2:A10 (down). In B2 type `=$A2*B$1` and fill right and down. Column A and row 1 stay locked correctly, building the whole table from one formula.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

scenes.text: An invoice shows the wrong price because a VLOOKUP returned the nearest match instead of the exact one.
One missing argument — FALSE — caused it.

steps.title: Syntax
steps.body:
`=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])`
- Looks in the **first column** of table_array, returns the value from column number col_index_num.
- **range_lookup = FALSE (or 0)** for exact match. If omitted, Excel assumes approximate match (TRUE), which needs sorted data and can return wrong results.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Price list in E2:G100 (Code | Name | Price). Code in A2.
`=VLOOKUP(A2,$E$2:$G$100,3,FALSE)` → price for that code. Lock the table with `$` before copying down.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- Can't look **left** (lookup column must be first).
- Column index breaks if someone inserts a column.
- Returns #N/A when not found — wrap with IFERROR if needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Omitting FALSE.
- Not locking table_array.
- Extra spaces or text-vs-number codes ('00123' vs 123) causing #N/A — clean with TRIM/VALUE.

steps.title: XLOOKUP
steps.body:
`=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])`
Exact match by default, looks in any direction, has a built-in 'not found' value. Available in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021+ (and in Google Sheets).

steps.title: INDEX/MATCH
steps.body: `=INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0))` — MATCH finds the position (0 = exact), INDEX returns the value at that position. Works in all Excel versions, any direction, and doesn't break when columns are inserted.

steps.title: Solved example: ID to the left
steps.body:
IDs in A2:A500, names in B2:B500, name to find in E2.
**XLOOKUP:** `=XLOOKUP(E2,B2:B500,A2:A500,"Not found")`
**INDEX/MATCH:** `=INDEX(A2:A500,MATCH(E2,B2:B500,0))`

steps.title: IFS and nested IF

steps.title: The basic query
steps.body:
```
SELECT column1, column2
FROM table
WHERE condition
ORDER BY column DESC;
```
- `SELECT *` returns all columns (avoid on big tables).
- WHERE operators: = <> > < >= <=, `AND`, `OR`, `IN ('North','East')`, `BETWEEN 100 AND 200`, `LIKE 'A%'` (starts with A), `IS NULL`.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:

`SELECT rep, amount FROM sales WHERE region = 'North' ORDER BY amount DESC;`
Returns North reps from highest to lowest amount.

steps.title: Order of writing vs running
steps.body: You write SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY, but the database logically runs FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY. That's why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE in most databases.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Text values need single quotes: 'North'.
- `= NULL` never matches — use `IS NULL`.
- Forgetting ORDER BY and assuming rows come back sorted.

lessons.title: Triple constraint and life cycle

steps.title: The triple constraint
steps.body: **Scope, time and cost** are linked, with **quality** in the middle. Change one and at least one other must change — or quality suffers. Modern guides also stress risk, resources and value.

steps.title: Project life cycle
steps.body: Initiating (charter, objectives, sponsor) → Planning (scope, schedule, budget, risks) → Executing → Monitoring & Controlling (throughout) → Closing (handover, lessons learned). **Predictive (waterfall)** plans up front; **adaptive (agile)** plans in iterations; **hybrid** mixes both.

steps.title: Solved example: a scope change
steps.body: Client adds two reports (scope ↑). Options: extend deadline by 2 weeks (time ↑), add a developer (cost ↑), or drop a lower-priority feature (scope swap). Record the decision through **change control**.

steps.title: Project charter
steps.body: Authorises the project: purpose, objectives, high-level scope, milestones, budget, sponsor, key risks, success criteria. No charter = no clear authority.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Scope creep': accepting small additions without assessing impact.
- No sponsor or unclear success criteria.
- Skipping the closing phase and lessons learned.

story.title: 'Build the app' is not a task

steps.title: Work Breakdown Structure
steps.body: A **WBS** breaks the total scope into deliverables, then smaller **work packages** that can be estimated, assigned and tracked. The **100% rule**: the WBS includes all the work — and only the work — in scope.

steps.title: Estimation techniques
steps.body:
- **Analogous:** based on similar past projects (quick, rough).
- **Parametric:** rate × quantity (e.g. 2 days per screen × 15 screens).
- **Bottom-up:** estimate each work package and add up (most accurate, slow).
- **Three-point (PERT/beta):** E = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6, where O = optimistic, M = most likely, P = pessimistic.

steps.title: Solved example: PERT
steps.body:
Task: O = 4 days, M = 6 days, P = 14 days.
E = (4 + 4×6 + 14) ÷ 6 = (4 + 24 + 14) ÷ 6 = 42 ÷ 6 = **7 days**.
Standard deviation ≈ (P − O) ÷ 6 = 10 ÷ 6 ≈ 1.7 days.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Estimating only the 'happy path'.
- Forgetting testing, reviews, deployment and documentation.
- Treating estimates as promises — communicate ranges.

steps.title: Critical path method
steps.body: Draw tasks with durations and dependencies. The **critical path** is the **longest** path through the network; it sets the minimum project duration. Tasks on it have **zero float** — any delay delays the project. **Float (slack)** = how much a task can slip without delaying the project.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
A (3 days) → B (4) → D (2); A → C (6) → D.
Paths: A–B–D = 3+4+2 = 9; A–C–D = 3+6+2 = **11**.
**Critical path:** A–C–D, **11 days**. Float of B = 11 − 9 = **2 days**.
If B slips 1 day → no impact; if C slips 1 day → project becomes 12 days.

steps.title: Gantt charts and milestones
steps.body: A **Gantt chart** shows tasks as bars on a timeline with dependencies. **Milestones** are zero-duration checkpoints (e.g. 'UAT sign-off'). Compressing schedules: **crashing** (add resources to critical tasks, costs more) or **fast-tracking** (do tasks in parallel, adds risk).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding people to non-critical tasks to 'speed up' the project.
- Ignoring dependencies across teams.
- Forgetting that the critical path can change as tasks slip.

steps.title: RAID log
steps.body:
- **Risks:** uncertain future events that may affect the project (probability × impact).
- **Assumptions:** things believed true but not confirmed.
- **Issues:** problems happening now.
- **Dependencies:** things your project relies on (or that rely on it).
Each entry has an owner, date and action.

steps.title: Risk responses (threats)
steps.body:
- **Avoid** (change plan to remove it)
- **Mitigate/reduce** (lower probability or impact)
- **Transfer** (insurance, contract terms, outsourcing)
- **Accept** (actively: with contingency; or passively)
- **Escalate** (outside your authority)

steps.title: Solved example: score and respond
steps.body:

Response: **mitigate** — weekly vendor check-ins, a mock API so the team can keep building, and an alternative vendor shortlisted. Owner: integration lead. Review weekly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing risks (may happen) with issues (happening now).
- A risk register filled once and never reviewed.
- No owner for each risk.

steps.title: Agile Manifesto (2001): four values
steps.body:
We value:
- **Individuals and interactions** over processes and tools
- **Working software** over comprehensive documentation

steps.title: A few of the 12 principles

steps.title: Three accountabilities (Scrum Guide 2020)
steps.body:
- **Product Owner:** maximises product value; manages and orders the **Product Backlog**; one person (not a committee).
- **Scrum Master:** accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness; coaches the team and organisation in Scrum; removes impediments.
- **Developers:** create a usable Increment each Sprint; own the Sprint Backlog.
The **Scrum Team** is typically **10 or fewer** people, with no sub-teams or hierarchies.

steps.title: Three artifacts and their commitments

An item is part of an Increment only when it meets the Definition of Done.

steps.title: User stories (a common practice, not required by Scrum)
steps.body:
Format: **As a** [user], **I want** [goal] **so that** [benefit].

steps.title: Story points and velocity
steps.body:
Many teams estimate relative size in **story points** and track **velocity** = points completed (meeting Definition of Done) per Sprint. Use the **average of recent Sprints** to forecast. Velocity is for the team's planning — not for comparing teams or judging people.
Example: last 3 Sprints = 28, 32, 30 → average **30**. Remaining backlog 150 points → about **5 Sprints**.

steps.title: Kanban basics

- Converting story points to hours.
- Counting partially done stories in velocity.
- No WIP limits → everything 'in progress', nothing done.
